articles.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in Party
articles.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.

blocks.text: Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This years plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past Plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This Plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

The STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Mixed fuel price adjustments will take effect Tuesday, October 27, with diesel and kerosene becoming more expensive while gasoline prices decline.
The Department of Energy announced the following changes Monday:

items: Diesel — up P1.20 per liter
Gasoline — down P0.30 per liter
Kerosene — up P0.50 per liter

blocks.text: The adjustments will remain in effect until Monday, November 2.
Last week, diesel prices rose by P2.60 per liter, while gasoline and kerosene prices fell by P4.30 and P1 per liter, respectively.
Industry forecasts late last week had pointed to larger adjustments for both diesel and gasoline.
Global supply pressures
The DOE said this week's price movements were mainly influenced by global oil prices amid supply pressures linked to conflict in the Middle East.
At the Singapore International Energy Week, Saudi Arabia announced an arrangement to store crude oil at Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns beginning in mid-2027.

"This arrangement enhances the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain in Southeast Asia, as well as contributes to Singapore's energy security and resilience in the event of supply disruptions," Singapore Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry Tan See Leng said.

Saudi Arabia's Minister of Energy and Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources Prince Abdul Aziz Bin Salman Al Saud also reaffirmed the kingdom's commitment to maintaining reliable energy supplies despite tensions in the region.
"Bringing supply closer to key Asian markets would strengthen the flexibility of our supply network and support Singapore's security of supply and preparedness," Al Saud said in a video recording.
The Singapore International Energy Week runs from October 26 to 30.

articles.title: 'Modus'?: Ombudsman urges DOJ probe into Philip Lustre arrest process
articles.summary: Lustre's lawyer said the journalist never received a subpoena or notice before his arrest.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 3:03pm

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has called on the Department of Justice (DOJ) to investigate the circumstances that led to veteran journalist Philip Lustre's arrest after his lawyer said he never received a subpoena or notice about the cyberlibel complaint against him.

In an interview with reporters on Monday, October 26, Remulla, a former justice secretary, pointed to a known "modus" in which complainants deliberately provide prosecutors with the wrong address of a respondent.

"Ano iyan, may modus kasi iyan. 'Yung mga nagfa-file ng kaso, binibigyan ng wrong address ang prosecutor," Remulla said after the signing of a memorandum of understanding with the Justice Sector Coordinating Council at the Supreme Court.
("There's a modus there. Those filing cases give prosecutors the wrong address.")
"Kailangan diyan maimbestigahan ng DOJ 'yan. Kung ano nangyari kasi nga bakit hindi dumating? Ano nangyari sa subpoena? Ano nangyari sa documents na pinadala sa respondent-accused?" he added.
("The DOJ needs to investigate what happened. Why didn't it arrive? What happened to the subpoena? What happened to the documents sent to the respondent-accused?")
Remulla said prosecutors should not merely rely on information provided by complainants and have a duty to exercise due diligence.
"It should not happen," Remulla said, referring to the circumstances raised in Lustre's case.
Arrested over cyber libel. Lustre, a veteran journalist, was arrested while attending a news forum in Quezon City on Saturday, October 24.
He was arrested on the strength of a warrant issued by the Regional Trial Court Branch 10 in Davao City in connection with a cyber libel case.
According to Lustre's lawyer, Dino de Leon, the journalist was unaware of the complaint before his arrest.
De Leon said Lustre had not received a subpoena or notice that would have given him an opportunity to answer the complaint during the preliminary investigation.

articles.title: [New Rx] The Philippines is getting older. What if we treated experience as an asset?
articles.summary: Rather than treating retirement as the expiration of professional value, the Philippines should create markets to harness the accumulated expertise and judgment of older workers as a productive…

blocks.text: The Philippines still thinks of itself as a young country. For decades, our demographic advantage has meant millions of young workers entering the labor force, staffing BPO offices, hospitals, factories and businesses here and abroad.
That advantage will not last forever.

According to the 2024 Census of Population from the Philippine Statistics Authority, 11.42 million Filipinos were already aged 60 or older in 2024, representing 10.2% of the household population. In 2020, the share was only 8.5%. PSA population projections suggest that by 2055, people aged 60 and above could account for about 19.6% of the population. PSA population projections
Almost every discussion of this transition begins with the costs.
More pensions. More chronic diseases. More hospital care. Greater demand for long-term care. Fewer working-age people supporting more retirees.
Those concerns are real. But they also encourage us to think about older people mainly as liabilities on the national balance sheet.
What if we looked at the other side?
A Filipino does not wake up on his 60th birthday having suddenly lost 35 years of accumulated knowledge, professional relationships and judgment.

Consider a 63-year-old physician. She may no longer want hospital nights, a full clinic or a 60-hour workweek. But she could spend 10 hours a week reviewing clinical cases for an international research organization. She could evaluate medical charts, mentor younger physicians, advise a biotechnology company, review drug-safety reports or teach clinical reasoning.

A retired nurse could train virtual-care teams. A former pharmaceutical executive could advise several startups. A retired banker could sit on investment committees. A former regulator could guide companies through systems that took him decades to understand.
What these people possess is difficult to manufacture quickly: judgment, networks, institutional memory, pattern recognition and credibility.
These are not simply social assets. They have economic value.
Some countries have already recognized pieces of this problem.

In Singapore, the government raised the statutory retirement age to 64 and the re-employment age to 69 from July 2026. Eligible employees must be offered re-employment, while programs such as the Senior Employment Credit subsidize employers who retain older workers. Singapore has explicitly described the objective as allowing seniors to remain productive while helping employers retain experienced workers. Singapore Ministry of Manpower on senior re-employment

Japan has gone further in encouraging continued employment. Its latest policy framework sets targets to raise employment among people aged 60 to 69 and expand measures allowing people to work until 70. It also supports job matching through public employment services and the country’s long-established Silver Human Resources Centers. Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare policy on older workers
These are important models.
But they still largely approach aging through the lens of employment longevity: how to keep older people in work, improve retirement adequacy and reduce the economic pressures of an aging society.
There is a further step the Philippines could explore.
Instead of simply asking how older workers can stay employed longer, ask how their accumulated expertise can be organized, matched with demand, digitized and sold as an economic service.
In other words, treat experience itself as a productive national asset.
Technology now makes that increasingly possible.
A person does not have to choose between a 50-hour workweek and complete retirement. Someone could work five hours a week. Ten hours. One project every quarter. One board meeting a month.

A retired specialist in Manila could review clinical data from the United States. A former executive in Cebu could advise a Singapore company remotely. A Filipino professional who spent 30 years overseas could mentor local entrepreneurs without permanently relocating home.
The objective should not be to force older Filipinos to work longer.

People who have worked for decades deserve pensions, healthcare and the freedom to stop working. Some will have health conditions that make continued employment difficult. Others will simply want retirement.
The goal is productive choice.
Those who remain healthy, capable and interested should not discover that the economy has no use for them unless they return to a conventional full-time job.

The World Health Organization itself cautions against equating aging with loss of productivity or contribution. WHO notes that older people contribute through paid and unpaid work, caregiving, communities and the transfer of knowledge, and argues that spending that enables their participation should be considered an investment rather than simply a cost. WHO on ageing, productivity and contribution
Artificial intelligence may make this opportunity even more important.
AI can summarize a medical chart. But an experienced physician may recognize that it missed the one detail that changes the diagnosis.
AI can generate a regulatory document. Someone who has dealt with regulators for 30 years may know which apparently minor sentence will create problems later.
AI can produce a financial model. An executive who has lived through several crises may recognize assumptions that look mathematically correct but make no commercial sense.
As machines become better at routine work, human judgment may become more valuable, not less.
Healthcare offers an obvious opportunity for the Philippines to test this idea.

The Philippines already had an estimated $4.2-billion healthcare-services outsourcing industry employing around 190,000 people in 2024, according to government industry-promotion materials. Its activities already include clinical support, medical coding, chart abstraction, data management and clinical-trial monitoring. CITEM’s Healthcare Philippines industry report

At the same time, the broader Philippine IT-BPM industry now employs about 1.9 million workers and generates more than $40 billion in annual revenue. IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines

The next evolution of healthcare outsourcing could require less repetitive processing and more clinical judgment, pharmacovigilance, research support, medical review, regulatory affairs, real-world evidence and AI supervision.
That creates an unusual opportunity for older professionals.
A global pharmaceutical company may value a Filipino physician with 30 years of oncology experience for five hours a week more than another full-time junior processor.
A startup may not be able to hire a former hospital CEO, but it could afford her expertise several hours a month.
A young physician entering clinical research may gain enormously from someone who has spent decades navigating hospitals, ethics boards, regulators and professional societies.

Imagine a national marketplace through which Philippine and foreign companies could find retired or semi-retired Filipino doctors, scientists, engineers, accountants, bankers, teachers and executives for fractional assignments.

Professional societies could maintain expert networks. Universities could create senior-fellow pools. BPO companies could develop global expertise-as-a-service businesses. Retired Filipinos abroad could participate remotely.
Instead of exporting only Filipino labor, the Philippines could increasingly export Filipino judgment.

The benefits would extend beyond another paycheck. Older people could maintain income and engagement if they want it. Younger workers gain mentors. SMEs gain access to expertise they could never afford full time. Professional networks are transferred rather than disappearing. Decades of accumulated human capital remain inside the productive economy.
The traditional demographic equation is simple:
More older Filipinos = more healthcare + more pensions + greater dependency.
That equation is incomplete.
There is another side:
More experienced Filipinos = more knowledge + networks + mentorship + productive capacity.
Both are true.

Countries such as Singapore and Japan have institutionalized important parts of senior employment. The Philippines can learn from them, but it can also go further: not simply extending working lives, but deliberately creating markets for what older people know.
That distinction matters because the Philippines is likely to age while it is still trying to become a much wealthier country.

We cannot afford an economy in which millions of people spend four decades accumulating expertise and then, because they cross an arbitrary age threshold, most of that economic capital becomes invisible.
The challenge is not to make Filipinos work forever.
It is to stop treating experience as something that expires at retirement.
An aging population will cost the Philippines money.
The more interesting question is how much value the country is allowing to retire with it. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

articles.title: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes
articles.summary:
Families forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before election

Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little…
articles.byline: Julian Borger, Sufian Taha and Quique Kierszenbaum in Hebron

blocks.text: Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.

A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.

Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.

As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.

The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.

blocks.caption: Fahed Ahmaro, who was forced to flee his home in the Deir Baha area of Hebron by Israeli security forces, looks at his house from a distance.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.

“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”

blocks.caption: Fahed Ahmaro’s house in Hebron, now a military position, with netting over its upper floors Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.

The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.

“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”

By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.

“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.

blocks.caption: Wasam Sadi, a Palestinian driver, has difficulties with his vision after he was attacked in his truck by Israeli settlers near the entrance of Hebron.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.

“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

articles.title: Man found dead in Queensland floodwaters as state hit by days-long deluge
articles.summary:
Many rivers and roads left flooded after torrential downpours across Queensland

A man’s body has been found in floodwaters following an unusual weather system that delivered multiple storms…

blocks.text: A man’s body has been found in floodwaters following an unusual weather system that delivered multiple storms and a days-long deluge to parts of Australia.
Emergency services were called to a creek at Boompa on Queensland’s Fraser Coast shortly after 11am on Monday after reports a man had been found unresponsive.
The man was declared dead after being found in Smothering Creek on Boompa Road, Queensland Police said.
An investigation into his death has begun, with police to prepare a report for the coroner.
Further south, six campers were rescued after becoming stranded by floodwaters at a public campground in Leyburn in Queensland’s Southern Downs.
Queensland Fire and Rescue Swiftwater crews responded to the call for help at 7.45am on Monday.
They rescued three men aged 71, 47 and 26 and two women aged 68 and 26 without incident around 11.15am.
There were no reports of physical injuries, Queensland Police said in a statement.
Torrential downpours across Queensland between Thursday and Monday left many rivers and roads flooded across the state’s south and east.
There are warnings of more rain and flooding to come.
Flash flooding hit Laidley Creek and Glenore Grove in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, closing some roads, Queensland police said on Monday.
The highest recorded four-day totals were spread across the state, with Blackdown Tableland, near Rockhampton, recording 439.4mm to early Monday.
Lower Springbrook, near the Gold Coast, recorded 325.2mm, while Nambour, near the Sunshine Coast, copped 314.2mm.
Brooweena, inland of K’gari, received 299.6mm.
Meteorologist Angus Hines said the system behind the downpours was unusual.

“The widespread rain bands with heaps of cloud cover, much cooler temperatures, and then the storms in that situation are really driven by what’s going on in the higher parts of the atmosphere,” he said.
On Sunday evening, thunderstorms were briefly connected from southern Queensland to Bass Strait, as a swift-moving system passed towards Australia’s east coast.
The storm band raced over most states, propelled by strong winds in the upper atmosphere.
“But that steering wind sort of just tapered off through the night last night over [Queensland’s] Darling Downs,” Hines said.
Flood warnings are current for Warrill Creek and the Bremer River in the Lockyer Valley, the Macintyre and Moonie rivers in the south, and the Mary River near the Sunshine Coast.
Western Queensland also remains on alert, with warnings current for the Warrego River at Charleville, the Bulloo River in Quilpie, and the Barcoo River at Blackall.
The Bureau of Meteorology said Queensland’s weather was set to return to more typical spring conditions as the week continued.
Hot and humid days are expected to give way to more subdued afternoon showers and storms.

articles.title: [EDITORIAL] Post-Lustre arrest: Decriminalize libel and cyber libel
articles.summary: Hindi na ito policy debate, this is crucial for the survival of Philippine democracy

blocks.text: Hindi na ito policy debate, this is crucial for the survival of Philippine democracy
Nitong Sabado, inaresto si Philip Lustre Jr., isang beteranong mamamahayag at may akda ng Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines.

Diin sa salitang Sabado — dahil palatandaan ito ng harassment — lalo na kung ang pag-aresto ay nakatali sa malayong korte tulad ng Davao City. Halimbawa, kung inaresto ka ng gabi ng Biyernes, Sabado, o Linggo, kahit pa may naka-duty na judge sa isang night court, malaki ang probability na ilang gabi kang matutulog sa kulungan, lalo na kung hahagilapin o ire-request mo pa sa ibang ahensiya o barangay ang required papers.
Maraming red flag na weaponization ng batas ang pag-aresto kay Lustre.
First red flag: Ginamit ang paboritong batas ng mga bully: ang cyber libel law. Ito rin ang ginamit laban kay Maria Ressa at Reynaldo Santos ng Rappler.

Nito lang nakaraang linggo, nag-file ng cyber libel complaint ang kapatid ni Bise Presidente Sara Duterte, si Davao Congressman Paolo Duterte, laban sa mga opisyal, staff, at reporter ng GMA 7. Inihain ang complaint dahil sa istoryang inilabas ng network tungkol sa graft case ng magkapatid na may kinalaman sa whistleblower na si Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Second red flag: Secret warrant. Walang notification ng complaint mula sa prosecutor, at lightning arrest ang nangyari. Under normal procedure, inaabisuhan ang aarestuhin, at may right of reply ang subject ng complaint.
Third red flag: Unknown case filed by an unknown complainant. Ang tanging alam ng kampo ni Lustre ay ang korte at hukom na naglabas ng arrest warrant — si Davao City Judge Retrina Fuentes.

Si Fuentes ang siya ring judge na naglabas ng warrant noong 2022 laban kay Walden Bello, isang academic at dating congressman, dahil sa umano’y cyber libel na nagmula sa reklamo ni Jefry Tupas, long time aide ng Bise Presidente.
Classic intimidation tactic ito ng media — kahit bailable ang kaso mo, ipatitikim ng complainant sa ’yo ang pait na makulong kahit isang gabi lang.

Kapag nasisilayan ng liwanag ng investigative journalism ang korupsiyon at pang-aabuso ng kapangyarihan, madalas ginagamit ang batas na punyal ng personal na vendetta, imbes na kalasag para sa pangangalaga ng publiko.
Desperado ba ang mga Duterte na agawin ang naratibo lalo ngayong tila hindi pumapabor sa Bise Presidente ang daloy ng paglilitis sa impeachment trial niya?
Nagshi-shift na ba ang mga anak ni Rodrigo Duterte mula sa victimhood narrative sa paborito ng ama nilang fear tactics?
Matagal nang panawagan ng Rappler ang decriminalization of libel.
Noong 2012, nanindigan ang Rappler na ang criminalized libel at cyber libel ay banta sa free speech at press freedom. Lalo nang pinatunayan ‘yan ng kasaysayan.
Decriminalize libel and cyberlibel. Hindi na ito policy debate, this is crucial for the survival of Philippine democracy.
Habang pinapayagan ng batas na ikulong ng estado at ng makapangyarihang mga pulitiko ang mga mamamahayag — laging nanganganib ang press freedom sa Pilipinas.

Mula sa drug war killings ni Rodrigo Duterte, ang mga mansion ni dating speaker Martin Romualdez sa ibang bansa, hanggang sa pandarambong ng elected officials sa flood control corruption — lahat ‘yan ay nabunyag sa pamamagitan ng media.
Let media continue shining the light. Decriminalize libel and cyber libel. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Brazil keeps left: what Lula’s victory means for his country and beyond
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured victory in the presidential race, we look the implications for democracy, the environment and international relations

Good…

blocks.text: Good morning. Chances are you woke this morning to news of two momentous election results. In Serbia, a student-led movement has ousted the country’s long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić (which you can read more about here). And just hours ago, Brazil’s president staged a sensational turnaround against his far-right opponent after a nail-biting vote.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, won a forth nonconsecutive term as president, seeing off far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who spearheaded the radical populist movement built by his father and former president, Jair. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election.

After Bolsonaro’s surprise first-round victory earlier this month, the Workers’ party incumbent Lula pulled off a historic fightback – a consolidation of the democratic resurgence the country has enjoyed since he took office – and an early birthday present for the veteran leftist, who turns 81 on Tuesday.

But with Bolsonaro refusing to accept the result, the victory is a tense one. I spoke to the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips, who was in São Paulo at the Workers’ party vote count, to find out what the result means and what may lie ahead.
Weekend roundup

items: UK news | Two people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter the UK.
Crime | British police are recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving, as figures show consumption has surged across England.

France | Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

UK politics | Prime minister Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.
Aviation | Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘This is the crescendo of Lula’s incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career’

blocks.caption: This morning’s results were an unprecedented turnaround, according to election analysts. Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

blocks.text: When the results were declared just after midnight UK time, the choice of Brazil’s 159 million voters was narrow, but clear. The 80-year-old leftist received 51.79% of the vote to his rival’s 48.21% – about 4.3m votes – in what Lula called “a defeat for denialism”.
A visibly angry Bolsonaro has already refused to concede, citing a decision to extend voting for an extra two hours – although both sides had called for it, for different reasons.
The outcome was an unprecedented turnaround after a populist surge in first-round voting at the beginning of the month left Brazil’s progressives reeling.

In those early October elections, Flávio Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – putting the 45-year-old scion of the authoritarian clan in pole position: not once, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
In the intervening weeks, the polls tightened dramatically, putting Bolsonaro ahead by only fractions of a percentage point.

“This is the crescendo of an incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career,” Tom says. I can hear crowds of Lula supporters cheering in the background as we speak, and fireworks exploding. “It saw Lula go from rural poverty to union leader to the first elected working-class leader of Brazil, who has helped millions of people escape poverty and rode a commodities boom in his first two terms”.

For Brazil, a Lula win represents stability and the assurance that the country’s democratic future is secure, at least in the short term. “Over the past four years, Lula has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by more than 70%. He’s come to the help of the Indigenous people who live there. He’s cracked down on illegal mining,” Tom tells me. “It’s very positive news is that all this will continue.”
How did Lula turn things around?

“Bolsonarismo is a far-right movement … that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” Bernardo Mello Franco, a political columnist for the Rio broadsheet O Globo, told Tom earlier this month, pointing to a series of societal shifts have contributed to this.
Evangelical Christianity has expanded across Brazil in recent decades, with church leaders throwing their support behind the socially conservative policies favoured by Bolsanaro Sr and Jr.

Pro-gun Flavio Bolsonaro harnessed voter frustration at chronic levels of urban crime and violence. Despite being embedded in Brazilian politics for decades, he successfully portrayed himself as an anti-establishment outsider, using social media far more effectively than his rival.

And others believe he had significant help: a dozen watchdogs and research groups have published reports alleging that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign. The controversy grew after Brazils’ electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”, while the company called the allegations “false and unfounded”.

Progressives were galvanised after the first-round results revealed a record abstention rate of 21%, more common among Lula-supporting groups such as lower-income voters, and their focus sharpened on mobilisation. Millions joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s army”, which sent out daily instructions on how to make supportive content go viral. The 80-year-old incumbent, who only took ownership of his first smartphone in recent days, started posting to Instagram and TikTok. For the first time, the president’s digital reach overtook that of Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign was hit by a succession of scandals. In a revelation that made the UK’s partygate seem tame by comparison, last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of the 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party along with sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to cut deals with his father’s government.

Amid speculation that a comeback might be possible, at a million-strong rally on Copacabana beach in Rio on Saturday, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “We are going to turn this around!”
And so he did.
What role did Trump play in the election?

The US president has boasted about “lots of people that I got elected” in Latin America, styling himself as a kingmaker after a succession of right-wing candidates aligned with Washington have won power.

Although Donald Trump did not openly endorse Flávio Bolsonaro, his influence loomed large. Last year, he denounced the supreme court trial of his ally Jair Bolsonaro as a “witch-hunt”, imposing extraordinary 50% tariffs on Brazilian imports as retribution for what he claimed was political persecution.

Lula has styled himself as the country’s defender against Trump’s “colonial” designs. His victory consolidates a multilateral foreign policy and pragmatic approach to relations with the US, China and Russia. He has rejected invitations to join the controversial coalition of Latin American countries conducting military operations against drug cartels alongside the Pentagon, which would have resulted in much greater US involvement on Brazilian soil.

Furthermore, a win for pro-democracy campaigners in one country may serve to bolster international counterparts. As our senior international correspondent Julian Borger sets out in this compelling piece, along with the Brazil vote, a series of high-stakes elections in Serbia yesterday, Israel on Tuesday and the US next week are closely interlinked, and Lula’s win may have global ramifications, as leaders across Latin America and the world congratulate him this morning.
What does the result mean for the environment, in Brazil and beyond?

Last week, Tom travelled to Roraima, the northern state where Bolsonaro registered his best result nationwide. On his trip, he heard first-hand from Indigenous leaders and conservationists on why the populist’s success was causing panic.

His father’s environmentally devastating administration facilitated an illegal gold rush – turbo-charged by record global gold prices – that ravaged the Yanomami Indigenous reserve on the northern reaches of the Amazon.

When Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, the left-winger launched an environmentalist mission to expel the illegal miners, taking on the multibillion dollar extraction industry. Alongside wider green policies, he reduced deforestation in the Amazon to record lows.
“Tragically,” says Tom, “the environment only came up in the final presidential debate of this campaign.”

“Given that the Amazon makes up such a large portion of Brazil, and how important that region is to the global climate crisis, it’s amazing that it’s not been debated more. But people were voting more on economy, public security and culture war issues.”
In that final debate last Friday, Tom says that Lula “tried to show off the excellent, if incomplete, work that his government’s done in protecting the environment”.
Many will be relieved at Bolsonaro’s loss, as his vision for the Amazon was almost identical to his father’s.

While a Lula victory brings hope that these policies will continue, he will be working with a newly elected congress that features a record number of rightwing politicians hostile to Indigenous rights and environmental issues.
How will Bolsonaro respond?
after newsletter promotion
The immediate aftermath of the election results is likely to be fraught, warns Tom, with Flávio Bolsonaro saying it was “impossible to concede the election result”.

“The Bolsonaro response is exactly as I feared but I don’t think it will mean very much,” Tom says. “All these world leaders are now recognising Lula’s win and I don’t think Bolsonaro has a hope of overturning this result”.

Tom suspects that in the coming days Bolsonaro will head to the States, to avoid ongoing criminal investigations. “That’s not to say there might not be violence from his supporters, but his political career is done. The fact they’ve lost is a sign that the name ‘Bolsonaro’ is toxic for a slight majority of Brazilian people.”
The week to come

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Cory’s shearwater fledglings on Corvo Island in the Azores.  Photograph: Andrea Zanenga

blocks.text: Every autumn, Corvo Island in the Azores turns off its public lighting for a few key days to help fledgling seabirds fly to the ocean guided by the stars.

Since 2019, the 450 or so inhabitants of the smallest and most northerly island of Portugal’s Azores archipelago have switched off the lights for five nights to tackle the disastrous effects of artificial light on Cory’s shearwaters. The campaign started after the community noticed huge numbers of deaths among young shearwaters, who spend three months in their nests before attempting their first flight to the ocean. Many are fatally confused by the artificial glow of streetlights, and end up crashing on the streets of the island’s only village, Vila do Corvo. By going dark, the stars can be seen clearly, allowing the juvenile birds safe passage to the ocean.

articles.title: Angus Taylor criticised for ‘tone deaf’ response to alleged attack on Helen Haines
articles.summary:
Zali Steggall and Monique Ryan say Coalition leader was wrong to deny link between parliamentary debate and political violence

Angus Taylor has been criticised for his response to

blocks.text: Angus Taylor has been criticised for his response to the alleged attack on Helen Haines, with crossbenchers Monique Ryan and Zali Steggall labelling a speech by the opposition leader “tone deaf” and saying he did not “read the room”.

Parliament returned in Canberra on Monday, a week after an alleged attack outside the Indi MP’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs. A 43-year-old man has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated.
The episode has sparked debate about the safety of MPs and the state of the political environment, including the culture of parliamentary debates.
But the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, and the One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce have rejected calls for a change in practice to cool Australia’s political debate.
“In the past week, it has been suggested by some there is a causal connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence,” Taylor said. “I disagree with this view.
“The Westminster system is about settling differences through robust and rigorous debate, not violence.

“Importantly, we debate with adversarial vigour, but we never allow that vigorous parliamentary debate to spill over into violence. People who resort to intimidation and violence cross a line that must never be crossed.”

He said Labor had been correct to call out far-right extremism in Australia but called for all extremism to be rejected. He said judges should “come down harder” on people found guilty of intimidation or violence.
“Another thing we must do is celebrate Australia more readily. Too many Australians have been taught to feel guilty and shame about our country and about our history.
“Is it any wonder that some feel deep animosity towards our democracy, our institutions, and our nation?”
Joyce told News24 his thoughts and prayers remained with Haines and her family, calling the alleged attack “so unAustralian”.

“Unfortunately what we’re seeing in Australia and around the world is a change in dynamics,” Joyce said. “I think parliament has got its part to play but I don’t think it’s going to be a solution to the problem.
“The issues, such as the Palestinian march across the [Sydney Harbour] Bridge, the vindictive, arsenic type of rhetoric that we see in the public realm, these are all part of it.
“I think it’s foolish to think if question time changes, Australia changes. Not necessarily, in fact highly unlikely.”
Steggall, the independent Warringah MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said she was personally disappointed by Taylor’s speech.
“There is a link between our words and actions,” she said.
“I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn.

“To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, make sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of parliament.”
She said the same caution should be applied to media reporting, election advertising and social media posts.
Steggall referenced conversations with Haines’ husband, Phil Haines, in Canberra on Monday.
“His words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate,” she said.
“We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.”
Ryan, the Kooyong independent, called Taylor’s response “tone deaf” and “hugely disappointing”.
“If Angus Taylor doesn’t think that the words that we use matter, I don’t understand how he aspires to lead a political party,” she told ABC TV.
“If we can’t rise to the occasion now after something as unthinkable as what happened to Helen and think about how we behave in the house and in the public space … we’re never going to do that.”

articles.title: House increases DPWH budget for Sandro Marcos’ district by P4.3B – watchdog
articles.summary: The People's Budget Coalition flags nearly 7,000 DPWH projects worth P190 billion without published project attachments in the House-approved 2027 budget

blocks.text: KEY POST. Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos leads the floor after being elected House majority leader on July 28, 2025.
Sandro Marcos' Facebook
The People's Budget Coalition flags nearly 7,000 DPWH projects worth P190 billion without published project attachments in the House-approved 2027 budget

items: Ilocos Norte's 1st District received the largest increase in public works funding, with an allocation of P4.74 billion in the House-approved budget for 2027, up from P369 million in the original proposal.

Concerns were raised during a Senate hearing regarding nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion added by the House without published documentation, prompting calls for the Senate to veto these additions.

Other districts represented by top House officials also saw significant budget increases, with the second and third largest hikes going to Davao de Oro's 2nd District and Misamis Occidental's 2nd District.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The congressional district of House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos in Ilocos Norte received the biggest increase in public works funding in the approved House spending bill for 2027, according to a budget watchdog.

Based on the transparency portal of volunteer-driven civic technology movement BetterGov.ph, Ilocos Norte’s 1st District was allocated P4.74 billion in project lists from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in the House version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.
This is a significant increase of P4.38 billion from the P369 million that was originally proposed for the district in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

The NEP is also called the President’s budget, a proposal submitted annually by the executive to Congress. The House, which is constitutionally mandated to come up with an appropriations bill, may amend that proposal.
BetterGov.ph said its portal does not make allegations of irregularity or wrongdoing by a public official, and only compares changes between the NEP and the House GAB.

“The (district engineering office) mapping associates offices with legislative districts; it does not establish that a representative requested, sponsored, or controlled a project, or that each project lies in every district associated with its office,” the website disclaimer reads.
During a Senate hearing though on Monday, October 26, Ken Abante of People’s Budget Coalition flagged the increases.

“Nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion were inserted by the House without published project attachments,” Abante said, adding that many of these projects involve the construction of multi-purpose buildings.

“If there are no published documents, the Senate should remove them. The Senate should veto them,” he added. “Our concern is that the House has still not learned its lesson or felt any shame, despite our marches and rallies.”
Rappler has asked Marcos’ office why and how the House decided to increase public works funding for his district by billions of pesos. We will update this story once his office replies.

Second and third on the list are the DPWH offices in Davao de Oro’s 2nd District and Misamis Occidental’s 2nd District, whose budgets increased by P1.68 billion and P1.65 billion, respectively, in the House-approved budget compared to the NEP.
Also in the top ten are DPWH district offices which serve the constituencies of:

items: Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez (budget of DPWH district office he shares with another lawmaker increased by P1.58 billion)
House Speaker Bojie Dy (budget of DPWH district office he shares with another lawmaker increased by P1.52 billion)
House appropriations chair Mika Suansing (budget of DPWH district office she shares with another lawmaker increased by P1.15 billion)
Isabela 1st District Representative Tonypet Albano (DPWH district office’s budget increased by P1.08 billion)
Isabela 3rd District Representative Ian Paul Dy (budget of DPWH district office he shares with another lawmaker increased by P993 million)

blocks.caption: Summary from BetterGov.ph

blocks.text: The changes in the budget introduced by the House are not yet final, as the Senate may either approve or reject the amendments.
Any differences in the budget bills they pass would be reconciled in the bicameral conference committee. – Rappler.com

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Clips of Sara, Baste Duterte on impeachment trial dismissal are AI-generated
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has not dismissed the case against Vice President Sara Duterte and will resume the trial on November 9

blocks.text: Claim: Vice President Sara Duterte and her brother, Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte, said the Senate threw out the impeachment case against the Vice President and that the trial wasted public funds.

Why we fact-checked this: Two Facebook reels posted by the page “Duterte Supporters” on October 15 carry the claim. Both are staged to look like media interviews outside Malacañang Palace, with reporters and microphones from several networks.

The first video shows Sara in a black polo with a reporter asking, “Vice, ano ang masasabi mo? Binasura ng Senado ang impeachment laban sa ‘yo.” (Vice, what can you say? The Senate junked the impeachment case against you.)
She answers: “Isa lang ang masasabi ko. Nagsayang kayo ng milyon na pera para sa pansarili ‘nyong interes.” (I only have one thing to say. You wasted millions of pesos for your own interests.)

Meanwhile, the second post shows Baste in a black suit, saying: “Walang napala ang impeachment ‘nyo. Inurong na lahat kasi wala kayong ebidensiya laban sa kapatid ko. Sobrang laki ng budget ang nawala sa trial na ‘yan. Sinayang ‘nyo, mga buwaya.”
(The impeachment trial yielded nothing. Everything was withdrawn because you have no evidence against my sister. A huge chunk of the budget was spent on that trial. You wasted it, you crocodiles.)

Some commenters took the videos at face value and agreed with the statements, with some replying, “True.” Together, the two reels have drawn about 7,700 views, 230 reactions, 30 comments, and 47 shares as of writing.

The facts: Neither of the two made these statements. No news report, government livestream, or official press release records either of them saying these lines. The videos are AI-generated and carry no label disclosing this.
AI detection tools flagged the videos as AI-generated. Sightengine provided a 99% likelihood rating, while Hive Moderation returned scores ranging from 99.1% to 99.6%.

Impeachment trial: On October 13, Day 39 of the impeachment trial, prosecutors withdrew three of the four articles — misuse of confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats. The defense team objected while the Senate impeachment court approved the withdrawal.

The trial continues on Article II, which accuses the Vice President of amassing wealth disproportionate to her lawful income, failing to disclose assets in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth, and holding prohibited business interests. (READ: Dropping 3 impeachment articles vs Sara, who benefits?)
The trial is scheduled to resume on November 9, with the defense’s turn to present its evidence.

Presiding officer Senator Francis Escudero said on October 25 that the trial could be finished before year-end. Two-thirds of senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings at the time of the vote would be required for a conviction.

Trial expenses: On October 14, the Vice President’s spokesperson Paolo Panelo claimed that 20 trial days spent on two dropped articles cost about P500 million, or P25 million a day, with total expenses exceeding P1 billion.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian debunked the alleged P25-million daily cost as “completely untrue,” saying it represents the cost of running the entire Senate, regardless of the trial.

According to Gatchalian, impeachment-related expenses only cost P14.55 million over 44 trial days, or about P330,763 per day. These covered meals, supplies, overtime pay, and an outside venue for budget hearings. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar, who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies from the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Who is Giovanni Lopez, Marcos' new DPWH chief?
articles.summary: Atty. Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez will take the helm of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), a year after serving as secretary of the Department of Transportation (DOTr).

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 2:26pm
Atty. Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez will take the helm of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), a year after serving as secretary of the Department of Transportation (DOTr).
Malacañang announced Monday that Lopez would swap positions with outgoing DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon in a move supposedly aimed at "accelerating reforms and improving public service."

A lawyer and certified public accountant, Lopez was tasked by Marcos to “strengthen safeguards and institutionalize the reforms, turning them into rules, processes and systems that will keep serving Filipinos,” Malacañang said.
As the new DPWH chief, Lopez is also expected to accelerate the implementation of government infrastructure projects, including roads and bridges.
To recall, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. designated Lopez as acting transportation secretary in August 2025, amid a Cabinet revamp triggered by the flood control controversy.

Before his appointment as DOTr chief, Lopez served as the agency’s senior undersecretary for Administration, Finance and Procurement. In 2022, he also served as executive director of the Land Transportation Office (LTO).

In 2021, Lopez served as officer-in-charge executive director of the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB), while concurrently serving as undersecretary for Finance and chief of staff to then-Transportation Secretary Arthur Tugade.
Lopez was appointed director for Legal Service in 2017 before serving as assistant secretary for Procurement and Project Implementation that same year.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Ube is worth $595M globally. Why is Philippines capturing just $3 million?
articles.summary: Philippine ube varieties are spreading to overseas growers who are outpacing the country in meeting global demand.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 2:25pm

MANILA, Philippines — Citing the spread of Philippine ube varieties abroad, the head of a national ube industry group has called on the Department of Agriculture to strictly enforce the suspension on fresh purple yam exports.
Chester Velasco, president of the United Ube PH Federation, said neighboring countries have been acquiring fresh ube and cultivating the crop themselves.

"As of 2025, the global valuation is around $595 million, and our share is only $3 million. We're not the number one exporter of ube. That's the sad reality," Chester Velasco, president of the United Ube PH Federation, said on One News' "The Big Story" on Saturday, October 24.
Velasco also described attempts at what he called "food fraud," where ube grown in other countries is marketed as products of the Philippines.
"There are also instances where they market it as Philippine ube even if it was locally grown in China or Vietnam," Velasco said.
For Velasco, the export restriction, which applies only to fresh ube, should effectively counter smuggling. Processed products such as ube powder, extract and halaya may still be exported.
"They should be stricter in implementing the ban because, as you said, it's so easy to smuggle," he said.
These concerns come as global demand for the crop grows while local farmers face limited access to planting materials, making it difficult for the Philippine industry to keep pace.
The United States was the biggest market for Philippine ube products, accounting for nearly half of the country's exports that year.
China and Vietnam, however, have also expanded their own production to meet the demand, Velasco said.

"Unfortunately, our neighboring countries, like China and Vietnam, have been importing fresh ube and growing it. This is what they have been doing. Vietnam has really been aggressive in growing and producing ube," Velasco said.

To support its production in the Philippines, the U.S. Department of Agriculture recently announced a development award of $34.1 million. Implemented by US-based organization TechnoServe, the fund is expected to support 12,500 Filipino ube farmers over the next five years.
The project also complements a separate P300-million government initiative to expand production by doubling crop planting areas.
Struggle with planting materials, low prices
The lack of planting materials remains one of the industry's biggest constraints. These include seedlings, tubers, setts and tissue-cultured planting materials, Velasco said.
He explained that some farmers sell their entire harvest instead of setting aside portions of ube tubers for propagation, further constraining the next planting cycle.
The industry is also dealing with uneven access to buyers.
In Romblon, Velasco said the federation encountered farmers selling ube for as little as P20 to P40 per kilo, discouraging some from planting again.
To address this, the group is promoting contract-growing arrangements that assure farmers of buyers and agreed prices.
"When there's a sudden change, we stick with that price. When the price goes up, we can negotiate. But when it goes down, we don't reduce it," Velasco said.
He said the arrangement gives farmers greater certainty that their harvest will be bought and encourages them to continue planting.
The industry also needs to improve production standards and certifications to meet export-market requirements, including organic, halal, HACCP and good manufacturing practice standards, Velasco said.

The federation, formed about three months ago, brings together farmers, growers, processors, manufacturers, exporters, academe and government agencies in an effort to consolidate what Velasco described as a fragmented ube industry.

articles.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
articles.summary: Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme.

blocks.text: Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.
A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram, external said he had died "suddenly".
Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.
Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.
In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.
"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said, external. "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."
He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.
He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.
Between 2022 and 2025, he won three Emmy awards for outstanding voice performance in a number of TV series.

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, external, Channing Dungey, the chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: "Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.
"He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."

articles.title: Higher training costs for older workers risks plan to tackle youth jobs crisis, employers say
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Ministers planning overhaul of apprenticeship funding to increase cost of over-25s training, Guardian understands

Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing…

blocks.text: Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis.

The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead.

Drawn up before Wednesday’s budget, the proposal, which was first reported last week, is expected to form part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are unemployed.

The chancellor, John Healey, is widely tipped to announce measures to bolster opportunities for young people to help the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the country.
However, business leaders urged the government to reconsider the plan to make training older workers more expensive.

“It will just mean opportunities are shifted around instead of creating new ones,” said Robert Halfon, a former Conservative skills minister who is now the executive director of policy at the manufacturing lobby group Make UK.

“We agree that getting young people back into employment and training is a moral and economic imperative. But making it more expensive for employers to train older workers isn’t the answer,” he added.

Calling on Healey to “break the cycle” of cutting and reallocating the apprenticeship budget in England, Halfon said the system was already struggling to deliver what businesses and young people need.

“If the government is serious about getting young people into good jobs and giving industry the skills it needs, it should use that opportunity to grow the number of apprenticeships available rather than restrict training elsewhere.”

Andy Burnham has placed youth jobs at the heart of his agenda, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and plans to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.
With over-25s accounting for more than half of new apprenticeship enrolments, ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the system towards supporting more younger people.

Under the latest proposal, which is yet to be finalised, employers would be able to fund the full cost of an apprentice under the age of 25 using the money they contribute to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn-a-year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham has placed youth jobs at the heart of his agenda, including plans to reverse the drop in apprenticeships. Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing Street

blocks.text: However, for an older worker, they would face a “co-investment rule” whereby levy funds would cover 75% of the costs. The rest would need to be covered separately.
Employers have for years been told they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.
John Foster, the chief policy and campaigns officer at the CBI lobby group, said: “We can’t make skills a zero-sum game.

“While it is right to focus on supporting young people who are Neet into work, adult training also has a vital role to play in opening up entry-level opportunities and helping people adapt and update their skills mid-career, particularly as AI reshapes the workplace.”
after newsletter promotion

Ben Rowland, the chief executive of the Association of Employment and Learning Providers, said: “The key to any further changes to the apprenticeship system is to bring employers on the journey. Anything that is too abrupt or too quick significantly endangers that.”

Business leaders have been pressing Healey to use Wednesday’s budget to provide support with soaring costs amid the war in the Middle East, and have urged the chancellor not to add to the pressure on firms after Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions.

Kate Shoesmith, the director of policy and insights at the British Chambers of Commerce, said: “At a time when businesses are under pressure to improve productivity and drive growth, employers need greater flexibility and support to invest in skills at every stage of a person’s career.

“The best way to encourage more youth apprenticeships is to make it easier and more affordable for firms to take on young people by reducing the wider costs of doing business, rather than creating new barriers to training.”

Labour has been told its youth skills strategy risks failure without reform, after just 160 young people were enrolled into its foundation apprenticeship scheme in the first eight months. Ministers have an ambition for 30,000 starts over the current parliament.

Joe Dromey, the general secretary of the Fabian Society, said that while flexibility was important for business, the current system was skewed too heavily towards funding older, often already highly qualified workers.
“These will not be easy decisions, and some will be unpopular with businesses. But tackling youth unemployment means making difficult choices about where public funding is spent.”
A government spokesperson said: “It’s right that we focus on reversing the 40% decline in the number of young people starting an apprenticeship and give them the skills they need to succeed.

“That’s why we have reformed the system backed by £3.3bn to deliver 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people and support employers with a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16- to 24-year-old apprentice.
“The Milburn Review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

articles.title: Who is Vince Dizon, the returning DOTr chief?
articles.summary: Malacañang announced Monday that Vince Dizon will once again lead the Department of Transportation, a little over a year after he left the office to serve at the Department of Public Works and…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 1:31pm

Malacañang announced Monday that Vince Dizon will once again lead the Department of Transportation (DOTr), a little over a year after he left the office to serve at the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
Dizon first served in the Cabinet of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. in February 2025, when he was appointed as DOTr secretary, succeeding Jaime Bautista.
At the DOTr, Dizon was tasked by the President to enhance physical connectivity and make life easier for the commuting public.
Six months after, at the height of the investigation into the flood control scandal, Dizon was transferred to head the DPWH, following the resignation of Manuel Bonoan.

When he moved to the DPWH, he was ordered by the President to conduct a full organizational sweep of the agency and ensure that public funds were used solely for infrastructure projects in the country.
Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Secretary Lino Cayetano said that at the DPWH, Dizon was able to disrupt a system “that had protected waste and corruption for years.”
With this, Cayetano said thousands of projects have now been open to the public, and long-unfinished projects are now being completed.

Now that he is set to return to lead DOTr, Malacañang said that Dizon is expected anew to make the daily commute of Filipinos a little easier, as well as shorten the lines and get rid of the fixers at the Land Transportation Office.
Dizon was likewise tasked by the President to push the completion of critical mass transport projects, “so workers and students spend less time on the road and more time with their families.”
Before he joined Marcos’ Cabinet, Dizon was a key figure during the administration of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
He served as president and CEO of the Bases and Conversion Development Authority (BCDA) from 2016 to 2021.

He was also the deputy chief implementer of the National Task Force Against COVID-19 during the previous administration, and was the presidential adviser on flagship programs and projects. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Ombudsman to create budget watch team, study SC ruling on 2024, 2025 budgets
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday said he will create a team to look into current budget proceedings as well as the Supreme Court"s (SC) ruling that declared as unconstitutional the General…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 1:28pm

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday said he will create a team to look into current budget proceedings as well as the Supreme Court’s (SC) ruling that declared as unconstitutional the General Approrpations Act (GAA) for 2024 and 2025.

“Kaya nga ngayon we are starting the budget watch, pinapanood na natin iyan which didn’t happen before and dito with the decision, we will appoint a group, compose a group that will study the SC decision and the budgets that came with the decision,” Remulla said in an ambush interview.

(That’s why we are now starting the budget watch, monitoring it, which didn’t happen before. And in connection with the decision, we will appoint a group that will study the SC decision and the budgets that came with it.)
This came after the SC declared as unconstitutional the 2024 and 2025 GAAs due to budget increases made by Congress while it declared unconstitutional provisions under the 2026 GAA.
The SC also said that while the doctrine of operative fact applies, it does not shield authors, proponents, or implementors from criminal, civil, or administrative liability.
When asked about whether SC’s remark regarding the authors and implementors may lead to the President being held accountable, Remulla said that the action occurs inside Congress.

“Ang Presidente kasi just submits the bill, the proposed bill to Congress, the action goes on inside Congress and it’s very hard to follow the action, may kani-kaniyang tyempo sila eh especially those who are scheming, to add things and subtract things,” Remulla said.

(The President just submits the bill, the proposed bill, to Congress. The action takes place inside Congress, and it’s very hard to follow what happens because they each have their own timing, especially those who are scheming to add things and subtract things.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Former RAAF pilot who allegedly murdered wife was ‘love rat’ and ‘master manipulator’, jury hears
articles.summary:
Robert John Crawford on trial after wife found near ride-on lawnmower on their Toowoomba property

A former RAAF pilot was a “love rat” and “master manipulator” who staged his wife’s death…

blocks.text: A former RAAF pilot was a “love rat” and “master manipulator” who staged his wife’s death to make it appear a tragic accident, a jury has heard.
Robert John Crawford, 49, pleaded not guilty on Monday to murdering his wife Frances Elizabeth Crawford at Upper Lockyer on 29 July, 2024.
Her body was found near a ride-on lawnmower at the bottom of a retaining wall on their sprawling rural property west of Toowoomba.
Crawford murdered his wife in the context of a long relationship breakdown, prosecutor Chris Cook told a Brisbane supreme court jury.
The husband then embarked on a long campaign to make her death appear an accident, Cook alleged.
Four women with whom Crawford allegedly had affairs are due to be called as witnesses.
“He made out to be a man with good Christian values,” Cook said.
“However, his story did not match his behaviour.
“He was a man who lived a double life for a long time.”
Cook described Crawford as “a cheater, adulterer, love rat, philanderer and womaniser”.
The jury was told Crawford was not committed to the marriage, with the couple on the verge of divorce when the victim died.
The members were told Crawford was motivated to kill his wife because he stood to lose financially in a divorce settlement.
He wanted to retain possession of the couple’s house and did not want to split his superannuation.
The jury was told Crawford wavered between divorcing her husband and giving him the chance to prove himself to her and their children.
She had set her husband a detailed list of boundaries, including “deal breakers” that would lead to divorce.
The deal breakers included sexual or emotional infidelities, porn and masturbation, the court was told.
Justice Lincoln Crowley told the jury the prosecution would allege Crawford caused his wife’s death either by strangulation or blunt-force trauma.
The jury will be taken to the site of the alleged murder on Wednesday.
Justice Lincoln Crowley told the jury the viewing would help them to understand the evidence.
The trial is expected to hear from up to 47 witnesses over the next three weeks.
Crawford’s defence barrister has not yet delivered an opening statement.

articles.title: JSCC, Ombudsman team up to intensify fight vs. corruption
articles.summary: The Justice Sector Coordinating Council (JSCC) and the Office of the Ombudsman on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to strengthen interagency cooperation and address systemic delays…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 1:22pm

The Justice Sector Coordinating Council (JSCC) and the Office of the Ombudsman on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to strengthen interagency cooperation and address systemic delays in the fight against corruption.
The MOU was signed by Supreme Court Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, SC Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh and Justice Undersecretary Raul Vasquez.

In a speech, Gesmundo said the partnership would strengthen the justice system’s collective efforts to fight corruption by aligning the Ombudsman’s mandate with those of other justice sector agencies.
“We now enter a new phase, one that brings the fight against corruption more deliberately into our collective efforts to strengthen the criminal justice system,” he said.

“That is why our partnership with the Ombudsman is groundbreaking. The Ombudsman’s constitutional mandate to investigate and prosecute erring public officers complements the respective mandates of the JSCC agencies,” Gesmundo added.
The JSCC is composed of the Supreme Court (SC), the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).

According to Gesmundo, the agreement commits the parties to closer coordination, responsible information-sharing, policy development, capacity-building and efforts to address corruption-related cases and systemic challenges.
Meanwhile, Singh stressed that reforming the justice system requires collective action.
“No man or woman can change the system alone,” she said.
“Anyone who promises our people that he can change the system on his own is lying. He will fail. Because it takes an entire sector. And that is why we have the JSCC,” she added.
Remulla said his office sought to join the council's coordination mechanism as an active and contributing partner rather than merely as an observer.

Through the partnership, the Ombudsman sees opportunities to strengthen corruption prevention, address bottlenecks in corruption-related cases, improve secure information-sharing and digital systems, and build institutional capabilities to combat increasingly sophisticated forms of corruption, he said.

“Let me also be clear that cooperation does not diminish institutional independence. The Office of the Ombudsman will continue to exercise its constitutional mandate independently, just as every member of the JSCC must discharge its responsibilities,” Remulla said.
“Institutional independence and meaningful cooperation are not contradictory. They reinforce each other,” he added.—MCG, GMA News
