articles.summary: After months of delay, Vista Land celebrates its higher EBITDA despite a plunge in net income and a P5-billion gap between its Q3 2025 and FY 2025 net income figures

blocks.text: After months of delay, Vista Land celebrates its higher EBITDA despite a plunge in net income and a P5-billion gap between its Q3 2025 and FY 2025 net income figures

items: Vista Land and Lifescapes reported a 59% drop in net income for 2025, falling to P3.8 billion despite a 6% increase in EBITDA to P24.2 billion.
The company reported P35.8 billion in consolidated revenue, but gross profit from its residential business decreased by 18% to P9.7 billion.

There is a discrepancy between the reported net income and earlier figures, suggesting potential fourth-quarter losses or revisions, with the company providing limited financial details in its announcement.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Billionaire Manny Villar’s Vista Land and Lifescapes (VLL) finally released its long-delayed 2025 earnings figures on Monday, October 26, revealing a steep drop in net income despite higher operating earnings.

Its net income plunged 59% to P3.8 billion from P9.37 billion in 2024. The company, however, led its announcement with earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), which rose 6% to P24.2 billion from P22.82 billion, meeting what it described as “the company’s target for the year.”

Unlike net income, EBITDA excludes interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. This means it can rise even as the bottom line falls if these expenses increase, such as when a company faces substantial borrowing costs.
Vista Land also reported P35.8 billion in consolidated revenue, although gross profit from its residential business, after deducting direct costs, fell 18% to P9.7 billion.
More puzzling is its September 2025 quarterly report, which showed P9.46 billion in net income for the first nine months alone, more than double the P3.8 billion now reported for the full year.
This leaves a more than P5-billion difference, which suggests a substantial fourth-quarter loss, revisions to earlier figures, or some combination of both.

blocks.caption: Mark Villar switches camps. Minutes later, family’s troubled firms make their move.

blocks.text: What drove the divergence remains unclear, as VLL issued only a press release with selected figures, rather than its set of full audited financial statements. The company did offer one possible explanation, saying its results “reflect, in part, the recognition of interest expenses that were not capitalized into qualifying assets.”

Instead, Vista Land emphasized that it launched 46 horizontal housing developments worth an estimated P49.6 billion, mainly under its Camella flagship brand. Its reported assets stood at P376.8 billion at year-end.

The earnings release arrives after months of delays in reporting the company’s financials. Vista Land is among six listed companies linked to the Villar family suspended from trading for missed reporting deadlines.

On October 8, Vista Land, Vistamalls, and VistaREIT announced a board approval to release their 2025 audited statements. The disclosures came on the same afternoon Senator Mark Villar moved to the Senate majority, while his sister Camille remained in the minority.

But so far, Monday’s filing is still limited to a press release attached to an SEC Form 17-C, not the complete audited statements or annual report. It does not clear Vista Land to resume trading. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Labour urged to plug predicted £400m shortfall in overseas aid funding in 2027
articles.summary:
Official forecast indicates shortfall below 0.3% of national income in promised official development assistance

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on…

blocks.text: The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.

Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.

The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
after newsletter promotion
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.

The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.

The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.

The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

articles.title: Bayeux tapestry becomes pop culture hit as young people more keen to see exhibition than top films
articles.summary:
Monzo says 55% of cardholders’ British Museum payments in first hour of latest ticket release were by people under 35

A 1,000-year-old embroidery may be an unusual candidate for a pop…

blocks.text: A 1,000-year-old embroidery may be an unusual candidate for a pop culture moment, but young people are seemingly more willing to shell out for tickets for the Bayeux tapestry than spend money on Hollywood blockbusters.

In the first hour that the second round of tickets to view the tapestry were available last Wednesday, payments from Monzo cardholders to the British Museum reached £14,100 and were 48 times that of a normal Wednesday morning. More than half (55%) of those buyers were aged under 35.

This was double the opening mornings for this year’s blockbuster films: the critically acclaimed The Odyssey, at £7,000, and the box office smash hit Spider-Man: Brand New Day, at £6,300, according to the bank’s spending data for its 16 million customers.

Tickets for the Bayeux Tapestry, which is on display in England for the first time since it was taken to France in the 11th century, are significantly more expensive than the average cinema ticket, at £33 for standard adult peak tickets and £27 for off-peak. However, adjusting for the more expensive entrance fee – as well as the limited availability of tickets compared with a blockbuster movie – highlights the huge appeal of the tapestry.
after newsletter promotion

As a result, buyers spent five times more on average at the checkout than on Spider-Man’s opening morning, at £97 versus £19. By the time the Bayeux tickets had been on sale for two hours, Monzo customers had spent £30,500. Enthusiasm was such that many buyers were willing to travel from across the country for the once-in-a-lifetime event, with almost half of the buyers based outside London, and the furthest purchases coming from Glasgow.
Thousands joined an online queue to secure tickets when they went on sale at 10am on Wednesday, with spots selling out within three hours – beating the first wave, which sold out in 24 hours.

The frenzy has drawn comparisons with big pop cultural events such as Glastonbury festival and the Oasis reunion tour. The British Museum said the response to the tapestry going on display last month had been “extraordinary”, leading it to make changes to address lengthy queues for ticket holders, including banning visitors from taking photos.

The exhibition has received rave reviews for its meticulous display of the woven record of the Norman Conquest, which is treasured for its impressive technical prowess, skilful storytelling and historical value. The Guardian described it as “a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth”.

blocks.text: LOPEZ. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Transportation Secretary Banoy Lopez inspects the Metro Manila Subway Project’s tunnel boring machine breakthrough on September 23, 2026, connecting the southbound tunnel between the North Avenue and Quezon Avenue Stations.
DOTr/FACEBOOK
After serving in the Department of Transportation for nearly a decade, Giovanni 'Banoy' Lopez moves to the Department of Public Works and Highways

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Transportation Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez as chief of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), replacing Secretary Vince Dizon.
Dizon, meanwhile, returns to lead the Department of Transportation.

A certified public accountant and lawyer, Lopez will be tasked to institutionalize reforms in the DPWH, which has been marred by corruption issues, said acting Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano.

Lopez has been serving DOTr for nearly a decade. Based on available public information, he served as assistant secretary for procurement and project implementation and director for legal services in the DOTr in 2017.
He was then appointed as DOTr undersecretary for finance and chief of staff in 2021. In the same year, he became executive director (officer-in-charge) of the Toll Regulatory Board.
In 2022, Lopez became executive director of the Land Transportation Office.
From February to August 2025, he was senior undersecretary for administration, finance, and procurement of DOTr.
Marcos appointed Lopez as DOTr secretary in September 2025, after the post was vacated by Dizon.
Lopez hails from Tuguegarao, Cagayan. He finished high school at the University of Saint Louis Tuguegarao in 1996.
Lopez earned his accountancy degree as cum laude at St. Paul University Philippines. He studied law at San Beda University. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Birthkeeper who allegedly ‘groomed’ pregnant women to fear hospital could face criminal charges
articles.summary:
Victorian coroner hears Emily Lal told Stacey Warnecke that her ‘condition and mindset’ needed to be ‘solid’ to avoid a hospital birth

A birthkeeper who allegedly “groomed” pregnant women to…

blocks.text: A birthkeeper who allegedly “groomed” pregnant women to fear hospital could be referred to prosecutors to face potential criminal charges, a Victorian coroner has heard.

Stacey Warnecke died in September 2025 at Frankston hospital in Melbourne after giving birth at home and suffering a postpartum haemorrhage with birthkeeper Emily Lal by her side, having paid her $6,000 to support her throughout pregnancy.
Birthkeepers have no clinical training and operate outside the medical system.
The inquest into Warnecke’s death began in June, but closing submissions to coroner Therese McCarthy were delayed after a forensic analysis of Warnecke’s phone.

Hearings resumed on Monday, when Rachel Ellyard, in her role as counsel assisting the coroner, said that the completed analysis had revealed numerous messages, including in a group chat on the platform WhatsApp coordinated by Lal for women who were choosing freebirth. A phone call between Warnecke, a 30-year-old nutritionist and wellness influencer, and Lal was played to the court.

Ellyard said the phone evidence directly contradicted evidence from Lal, given in June, that she was hired by Warnecke primarily to play the role of a supportive friend, and that the money paid to her was primarily for her time, but not for medical advice.

“Ms Lal saw her role as to groom her clients into being strong enough to resist the temptation to seek medical help during labor, to seek pain relief during labor, to go to hospital during labor,” Ellyard said.

“It’s clear that Ms. Lal thought that in most cases, going to hospital would represent a failure of someone who hadn’t done the work, who hadn’t understood enough what the intensity of labor was going to be.”
During the call, Warnecke told Lal that she envisioned having a “wise woman” next to her during her first childbirth, to guide her when asking: “Am I dying, or am I alright?”
Warnecke told Lal she was afraid of the hospital.
Lal responded: “You should be scared of the hospital.”
“It’s a terrifying place. For me personally, I think the biggest, the key … to actually staying home and having your baby … is that your mindset and your condition needs to be so solid.”

Lal also told Warnecke that midwives who attend home births sometimes inadvertently sabotage them, because if the birth goes on too long, they tell the woman to go to hospital. This is sometimes just because the midwife is exhausted, Lal said.
She told Warnecke: “I manage my own energy as much as I can in that way, so that I don’t subconsciously sabotage a person.”

Lal previously told the court that she was not clinically trained, and that it was not her responsibility to make Warnecke’s birth safer, or to call an ambulance unless specifically asked. Lal said she never gave Warnecke medical advice, and only shared her own experiences of freebirthing her own children.

Ellyard said on Monday that given the evidence from the call and many messages and documents obtained from Warnecke’s phone, “the role that Stacey thought Ms. Lal would play during the freebirth … was to help her by keeping her safe”.
“Stacey was placing considerable reliance on Ms. Lal, in whom she had placed considerable trust.
“Ms. Lal was an expert. She was providing advice. She was providing referrals. She was selling supplements. She was offering commentary.
“This is all quite inconsistent with the idea of just being a friend who pulls your hair back and wipes your forehead. It’s something much more structured, much more deliberate.”
Ellyard said Warnecke’s husband, Nathan, had also been “reassured or indoctrinated into a sense that his role was just to just sit back and support, and that whatever Stacey experienced was alright”.
Lal was invited to return to court to give further evidence after the phone analysis, but had declined to, the court heard.
Lal only gave evidence previously on the condition that the Coroner grant her a certificate of protection so that her evidence could not be used against her in any future proceedings.

Ellyard put to the Coroner on Monday that it would be open to her to find that Lal had committed purgery “in relation to the falsity of the evidence” and to refer her to the Office of Public Prosecutions [OPP].
The OPP prepares and conducts criminal matters on behalf of the director.

“Having regard to the materials that have now become available … it would be open to your honor to form the view that Ms Lal wasn’t truthful in the evidence that she gave to you, and that a referral could be made in relation to the offence of perjury,” Ellyard said.

She said there was also evidence Lal had been “holding herself out as someone capable of giving such expert advice and capable of meeting the needs of pregnant women in a range of circumstances” despite having no authority.

The court previously heard that Lal had asked Warnecke three times whether she wanted an ambulance called after she gave birth to the placenta, lost up to 1.5 litres of blood, then began struggling to breathe.
Lal previously told the court that it was not her role to call an ambulance against her client’s wishes, even if the woman was unconscious and dying.
Warnecke said yes to an ambulance the third time, but by the time paramedics arrived she was seriously unwell, having suffered a massive postpartum haemorrhage.
Warnecke died in hospital several hours later from related complications, with the hospital exhausting its blood supply trying to save her.
Ellyard said on Monday: “Stacey would have survived if she was in hospital”.

Midwives and doctors know that postpartum haemorrhage is the most common complication of childbirth and are so well trained to identify it and treat it that “women do not die in hospital” from it in well-resourced countries, Ellyard said.
Warnecke also “would have survived if she was giving birth at home with a registered midwife,” Ellyard said, drawing from evidence given by medical professionals earlier in the inquest.
“She suffered a known complication of childbirth, which was eminently treatable if identified and responded to immediately.”
The coroner will deliver her findings at a later date.

articles.title: Australian murderer loses bid to eat Vegemite in prison
articles.summary: Andre McKechnie, who murdered a property developer, argued it was his right to enjoy Australian culture.

blocks.text: A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.
Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".
Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.
And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".

In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.
McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.
During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.
The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.
A much-loved breakfast spread for some, Vegemite has acquired controversial accolades since it first hit shop shelves in Australia in 1923.
The thick, brown spread was invented in the Victorian capital of Melbourne more than a century ago as an alternative to the British spread Marmite.

It sparked an international dispute in April last year when an Australian cafe owner in Canada was told to remove jars of the condiment from his shelves as it did not comply with local health regulations.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the row, saying it was "rather odd" that Canada allowed the sale of Vegemite's "rubbish" rival product Marmite. The cafe owner was later allowed to continue selling the spread.

articles.title: Old playbook vs Duterte critics resurfaces in journalist Philip Lustre's arrest
articles.summary: "They couldn’t find him" to serve the complaint, but police found him when it was time to arrest him.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 11:54am

MANILA, Philippines — The weekend arrest of journalist Philip Lustre Jr. followed methods long used to harass former President Rodrigo Duterte's critics, his lawyer said, pointing to a complaint filed far from where the accused lives and timing the arrest to block immediate bail.
Lawyer Dino de Leon, counsel for the 72-year-old, noted the "highly irregular" steps in the cyber libel case initiated against Lustre in Davao City, the political stronghold of the Duterte family.

Among others, De Leon flagged how Lustre did not learn of the charges against him until police arrived with a warrant for him in the middle of a forum on Saturday, October 24. De Leon, who was attending the forum as guest speaker, stepped in to represent him.
Denial of due process
De Leon said the prosecutor’s subpoena for the preliminary investigation was sent to a wrong address, depriving Lustre of his right to submit a counter-affidavit before the court ordered his arrest.
"Hindi siya mahanap, hindi siya matunton. Pero pagka-posas na, ang daling matunton," De Leon said in an interview with DZMM on Monday, October 26.
(They could not find him or track him down [for the subpoena]. But when it came time to handcuff him, he was easy to locate.)
De Leon criticized prosecutors for bypassing preliminary notice and argued that presenting an arrest warrant as a first notice violates basic constitutional protections.

"Hindi naman puwedeng posas ang una mong makikita," De Leon said. "May preliminary investigation, eh mali 'yung address... So pagdating sa subpoena para ma-make sure na may due process, na-depensa niya sarili niya, makapag-file ng counter-affidavit — wala."

(You cannot just present handcuffs first. There should be a preliminary investigation, but the address was wrong. So when it came to serving the subpoena to ensure due process and allow him to defend himself—nothing.)
He called on the Department of Justice to investigate whether Davao City prosecutors are routinely skirting the regular process to swiftly act on complaints by the Duterte family.

"Nananawagan kami sa Department of Justice na imbestigahan kung kalakaran ba ito sa Davao City Prosecutor's Office," he said. "Basta mga Duterte o mga Davao group ang nagrereklamo, wala nang due process?"

(We are calling on the Department of Justice to investigate whether this is standard practice in the Davao City Prosecutor's Office. Whenever the Dutertes or the Davao group file a complaint, is due process discarded?)
Calculated weekend arrest

Judge Retrina Fuentes of the Davao City Regional Trial Court Branch 10 signed the warrant on October 2. It charges Lustre with online libel under Section 4(c)(4) of the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012.
Police served the warrant on a Saturday morning when court offices were closed and processing bail would've been more difficult.
Lustre, a senior citizen who has difficulty walking, was held for hours and was unable to eat lunch while his legal team scrambled to secure his release, De Leon said.
Defense lawyers eventually located an emergency duty night judge late Saturday evening to process his P48,000 bail, allowing Lustre to avoid staying in detention through the weekend.
In a social media post after his release, Lustre called the arrest “a special operation” against him.
“The intention was to have me arrested on a Saturday and stay in jail on a weekend because I might not be able to post bail for my release,” Lustre wrote.
Police officers unable to explain warrant
De Leon also flagged the lack of knowledge by the arresting officers themselves who could not explain who had filed the complaint against Lustre.
While the warrant specified the offense as cyber libel, it omitted the private complainant's identity and specific facts.

De Leon explained that under the court system, warrants uploaded to the electronic e-warrant portal often lack attached case information. This leaves police officers unable to explain the basis of an arrest, as was the case on Saturday.
“Dapat sana in-upload ‘yung information para pag tinanong naman ‘yung pulis, ‘Bakit n’yo po ako inaaresto?’ eh may maisagot naman ‘yung pulis,” he said.
(The information should have been uploaded so that when the police are asked, “Why are you arresting me?”, they would have an answer.)
"'Di ba nagmumukhang katawa-tawa yung ating buong sistema, na 'gagawin lang po namin trabaho namin wala kaming kaalam-alam'?" he added.
(Doesn't our entire system look ridiculous — with the stance, 'We’re just doing our jobs; we have no idea about anything'?)
Filing venue
The complaint was filed in Davao City, nearly 1,000 kilometers from Manila, where Lustre is based.
Under the Revised Penal Code, a private individual may file a libel case where the material was first printed and published, or where he or she lived when it was published.
Lustre is the author of “Kill, Kill, Kill,” a book on killings during Duterte’s drug war.
Duterte is on trial at the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity over the drug war he carried out as president, and earlier, as Davao mayor.
Under Duterte
Duterte often attacked news organizations that reported critically on his drug war.
In December 2019, Duterte vowed to see to it that broadcaster ABS-CBN went off the air, a promise that his allies in the House delivered by 2020, when they rejected the network’s franchise renewal.

News site Rappler and its chief executive, Maria Ressa, also faced a string of criminal cases under Duterte. Ressa was arrested at her office one evening in February 2019, too late to post bail, and spent the night in custody.
She was convicted of cyber libel in 2020 and has appealed the case to the Supreme Court.
Media groups have long pushed for the decriminalization of libel in the country, where several such cases have been used to intimidate the press.

A United Nations special rapporteur has also backed calls to repeal the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, a highly contested law that rights groups say has been weaponized to go after critics of government.

articles.title: Gasoline prices get a rollback, diesel prices rise again on October 27
articles.summary: Continued tensions and possible escalations in the Middle East conflict continue to put pressure on global supplies

blocks.text: Motorists queue at a gas station in Paco, Manila, to take advantage of a ₱4.30 per liter drop in gasoline prices, on October 20, 2026, while diesel prices rise by ₱2.60 per liter.
Rappler
Continued tensions and possible escalations in the Middle East conflict continue to put pressure on global supplies
MANILA, Philippines – Gasoline prices are set to ease while diesel prices rise for a second straight week starting Tuesday, October 27.
The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the following permitted price adjustments for October 27 to November 2:

items: Gasoline – rollback of P0.30 per liter
Diesel – increase of to P1.20 per liter
Kerosene – rollback of P0.50 per liter

blocks.caption: Photo from Department of Energy briefing.

blocks.text: The adjustments follow last week’s movements, when gasoline prices dropped by P4.30 per liter and kerosene by P1, while diesel increased by P2.60 per liter.

The continued diesel price increases come amid tight international supplies, made worse by renewed attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and commercial vessels in the Middle East. Escalating hostilities involving Yemen’s Houthis have threatened alternative oil export routes, while tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continue to put pressure on global supplies.
Oil prices went up on Friday, October 23, with Brent crude rising 3.14% to $116.72 per barrel, its highest settlement in nearly six months.

Local pump prices remain substantially higher than before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, common Metro Manila prices stood at P56 per liter for RON95 gasoline, P54.70 for RON91, P55 for diesel, and P83.47 for kerosene.
The Philippines imports much of its petroleum requirements as finished products, making domestic prices vulnerable to changes in regional fuel markets, freight costs, and foreign exchange rates.

Meanwhile, excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene remain suspended under Executive Order No. 125, issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in September. The relief does not cover gasoline or diesel. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sandiganbayan allows 2 DOH officials to testify in Duque, Lao graft case
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan on Monday allowed two Department of Health (DOH) officials to testify in the graft case against former Health Secretary Francisco Duque III and former Budget Undersecretary Lloyd…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 11:20am

The Sandiganbayan on Monday allowed two Department of Health (DOH) officials to testify in the graft case against former Health Secretary Francisco Duque III and former Budget Undersecretary Lloyd Christopher Lao over the alleged illegal transfer of P41 billion in DOH funds to the Procurement Service of the Department of Budget and Management (PS-DBM) during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The anti-graft court’s First Division allowed Dawnavi Lacsado and Abegail Conchada, administrative officers of the DOH procurement unit, to take the witness stand despite the defense team’s motion to disqualify them.
The testimonies could help establish the officials’ respective roles in the DOH’s procurement operations and the work of the COVAC Secretariat during the pandemic.
Their accounts may also help clarify the extent of their involvement in procurement-related activities and the limits of their knowledge of the policy decisions at the center of the case.
Defense lawyers, however, argued that the officials’ testimonies would merely repeat those of other witnesses and violate the accused’s right to a speedy trial.
The prosecution maintained that the defense's urgent motion to disqualify the two officials had no factual or legal basis.
During cross-examination by the defense, Lacsado and Conchada confirmed that they were part of the COVID-19 Vaccination Plan (COVAC) Secretariat.
They, however, claimed they had no personal knowledge of policy-level decisions, such as whether the DOH should use its own procurement unit or the PS-DBM for its procurement requirements.
But when asked by the defense whether her role was limited to compiling procurement-related documents, Lacsado replied, “No.”
Conchada was also asked whether the COVAC teams operated with a skeletal or reduced workforce during the pandemic.
“The COVAC [teams] are all working,” she replied.

Conchada said the full team initially convened online during the pandemic, but the number of members required to attend each meeting was later reduced because of logistical challenges, including internet connectivity issues.
At the end of the hearing, the court granted the prosecution additional time to submit a compliance report explaining the purpose of presenting each of the 54 witnesses it had listed.
The prosecution also said it would submit the judicial affidavits of the witnesses it intends to present five days before the next hearing, scheduled for Nov. 9.
Duque and Lao are currently out on bail.
The succeeding hearings in the graft case are scheduled for Nov. 23 and Jan. 28, 2027.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Vince Dizon, Giovanni Lopez trade posts at DOTr, DPWH
articles.summary: Dizon is back to fix Filipinos' commute, while Lopez is tasked to sustain DPWH reforms.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 11:05am
Composite image shows file photo of Cabinet officials Giovanni Lopez and Vince Dizon.
PCO, file; Philstar.com composite
This is a developing report. Please check back for more details.

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has switched the heads of the transportation and public works departments, sending Vince Dizon back to lead his former agency and Giovanni Lopez taking his place.
Presidential Communications Office Secretary Lino Cayetano announced the changes at a press briefing Monday, October 26.
Dizon will return to the Department of Transportation, while Lopez, who had been serving as acting transportation secretary, has been appointed to lead the Department of Public Works and Highways.

"In the president's own words: 'We are shifting gears to accelerate reform. Secretary Dizon goes to DOTr to fix the daily commute. Secretary Lopez goes to DPWH to make sure the reforms there last,'" Cayetano said.

"Lahat ng ito, para lalong bumilis at gumaan ang serbisyo ng gobyerno para sa ating mga kababayan," he added. ("All of this is to make government services faster and easier for our fellow Filipinos.")

The appointments reverse a Cabinet reshuffle made in August 2025. Dizon, then transportation secretary, was appointed to lead the DPWH on Aug. 31, 2025, following the resignation of then-Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan amid controversy over alleged anomalous flood control projects.
Lopez, then a DOTr undersecretary, was appointed acting transportation secretary to take over the post vacated by Dizon.

articles.title: [Newspoint] Duterte’s Frankenstein monster
articles.summary: One problem remains intractable and self-compounding, and that problem happens to be the Frankenstein monster Rodrigo Duterte created for us

blocks.text: One problem remains intractable and self-compounding, and that problem happens to be the Frankenstein monster Rodrigo Duterte created for us

Lest we lose perspective in our preoccupation with Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, she is the anointed political heir of the man who brought untold horrors upon us when he was president — her own father.

And as though in too much hurry to prove herself deserving of the anointment, and with a sense of impunity that runs in the family, she got herself impeached even before she could go halfway through her term as vice president, the very first national office she has held. And impeachment being a dicey thing, wait till she is acquitted, thus retained in office and re-certified eligible to go for the heights of notoriety achieved by her father — or higher.

Her prosecutors appear confident, however, that she will be stopped. They have decided to pursue only one of the articles of impeachment and drop the other three. They made that decision after their final witness, a financial forensicist, had lent a strong close to their case on that one article — unexplained wealth. If they get her on that, she is removed automatically as vice president and barred from holding public office ever again.

But then again, in a court where senators, instead of professional judges, sit, politics is always a factor, making acquittal a realistic prospect regardless of the quality of the evidence. And how is this for political weight? Sara Duterte is polling the best numbers for the presidential vote in 2028. I confess I don’t quite get it myself, knowing that we need only look back on her father’s time to see what we’re in for if she does win.

Rodrigo Duterte’s presidency (2016-2022) was notorious across the board, but, for our purpose here — a quick, immediately relevant review of his treasonous, murderous, and corrupt regime — I have selected only a few cases, although cases sharply emblematic by themselves.

Our first case is his war on drugs, which took tens of thousands of lives by extrajudicial means and for which he was flown to The Hague, the Netherlands, to face trial before the International Criminal Court for “crimes against humanity.” That war was generally explained away as Duterte’s own sick “final solution,” but it is turning out to be sicker than that. Duterte may have had Hitler’s deeply unprincipled conviction, but, apparently, he was all business too.

Old and mostly hearsay allegations that his war was actually a coverup for his family’s own connection to the drug trade are gaining credence. Bank accounts held jointly by Rodrigo and Sara and submitted in evidence at the impeachment hearings have revealed payments from a drug-trafficking suspect.

The second case tends to show another unholy connection. Congressional and judicial investigations into the biggest corruption conspiracy in our history have also led to the Dutertes. The conspiracy involves over a trillion pesos in taxpayer money budgeted for flood control. Most of that money has been traced to the accounts of public officials as kickbacks and to those of private contractors as fees collected doing nothing or, at best, for doing token work.

The investigations have shown that the most audacious among the contractors — the couple Curlee and Sarah Descaya — had their start in Davao City, the Dutertes’ dynastic preserve, and that they also began to flourish there. The investigations have further shown that Rodrigo Duterte’s son Paolo received a generous PhP51-billion outlay for flood control for his district as its representative in Congress. Both the rise of the Descayas and the rain of fortune on Paolo Duterte came during his father’s presidency.

So well-oiled was the conspiracy that it went on for three more years after Duterte had ended his term. However, once exposed, under the succeeding government, the two cases began to be addressed with tighter administrative and systemic controls and more aggressive judicial prosecution.
But one problem remains intractable and self-compounding, and that problem happens to be the Frankenstein monster Duterte created for us.

Upon taking office, Rodrigo Duterte pivoted away from our traditional democratic partners and aligned his presidency to the dictatorial regimes of China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Soon enough, Duterte practically ceded our West Philippine Sea to China. It was a pact between betrayers: it came around the time that our claim to sovereignty over that sea was affirmed by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in a process to which China, the rival claimant, had itself agreed.

Duterte not only gave the Chinese control over traffic on that strategic waterway and access to its marine resources and minerals, but also facilitated the pursuit of their colonialist ends. Now, a decade later, they have established an effective full run over those waters, using a dedicated force of ships and planes to keep out our own navy and coast guard, our own marine researchers, and our own fisherfolk who had made their living there all their lives until Duterte made his treasonous deal.

And if you now ask his anointed, Sara, about it, she would tell you, with the arrogant confidence that only a well-funded and well-protected collaborationist can exude, that it is us who are the “troublemaker[s]” in the West Philippine Sea — us Filipinos, us the rightful sovereign!
Stand her against the wall? We can’t even put her on the stand! – Rappler.com

articles.title: Dizon returns to DOTr, Lopez takes over DPWH in Marcos Cabinet reshuffle
articles.summary: 'We are shifting gears to accelerate reform. Secretary Dizon goes to DOTr to fix the daily commute. Secretary Lopez goes to DPWH to make sure the reforms there last,' says President Ferdinand Marcos…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Vince Dizon is leaving the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) a little over a year after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. tapped him to lead the agency and address corruption concerns.
He is returning to the Department of Transportation (DOTr), which he previously headed.
DOTr Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez, meanwhile, will take over the DPWH. Lopez was appointed as DOTr chief after the post was vacated by Dizon in September 2025.

“We are shifting gears to accelerate reform. Secretary Dizon goes to DOTr to fix the daily commute. Secretary Lopez goes to DPWH to make sure the reforms there last. Lahat ng ito, para bumilis at gumaan ang serbisyo ng gobyerno para sa ating mga kababayan,” Marcos said, as relayed by Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano in a press briefing on Monday, October 26.
(All of this is to make government services faster and more accessible for our fellow Filipinos.)

Cayetano said Dizon is returning to the DOTr with the President’s “full confidence” and a mandate to make daily commutes easier, shorten queues at the Land Transportation Office (LTO), and get rid of fixers.
At the DPWH, Cayetano said, Dizon had opened thousands of projects to public scrutiny, pushed for the completion of long-unfinished projects, and begun reforms aimed at addressing corruption.

Meanwhile, Cayetano said Lopez, a lawyer and certified public accountant, will be tasked with institutionalizing these reforms by establishing rules, processes, and systems designed to ensure they endure.
In September, Dizon’s appointment was questioned by Senator Imee Marcos, as his appointment has yet to be confirmed by the Commission on Appointments.
Dizon has been candid that he wanted to vacate his post as DPWH secretary.

articles.title: Outsource Philippine visas? Ombudsman call draws DFA defense of mandate
articles.summary: DFA pushes back against Boying Remulla's call to outsource processing to third parties.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 10:43am

Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla responds to senators’ questions regarding the Philippines’ residual obligations to the International Criminal Court (ICC) following its withdrawal from the tribunal, during a public hearing on Thursday, April 10, 2025.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has called for Philippine visa processing to be outsourced to third-party providers, a comment which drew a sharp objection from the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Speaking on DZRH on Saturday, October 24, Remulla said foreign service officers should focus on diplomacy rather than handling visa applications.
"Ang problema ng DFA, they forget that their primary job is to be diplomats. Eh dito iba 'yung gusto nilang mangyari, gusto nilang magnegosyo," Remulla said.
("The problem with the DFA is that they forget that their primary job is to be diplomats. But here, they want something else to happen; they want to go into business.")

"Ako talaga ang stance ko diyan, let the Philippine visa processing be done by a third party, VFS (Visa Facilitation Services). Para alam natin kung sino pumapasok, nave-vet natin lahat ng pumapasok," he added.
("My position is to let Philippine visa processing be handled by a third party, like VFS. That way, we know who is entering and we can vet everyone coming in.")
Remulla argued that using a third-party provider would establish a uniform international standard for processing applications and screening tourists and business travelers.
"Kasi pag binigay sa VFS 'yan, it will become a standard of the country for the rest of the world," he said.
("Because if that is given to VFS, it will become the country's standard for the rest of the world.")
Remulla also said immigration matters should pass through the Department of Justice because of the need to conduct background checks on people entering the country.
"Dapat dumaan sa Department of Justice yan. I think so, because we want to get a background of the people entering our country," Remulla said.
("That should go through the Department of Justice. I think so, because we want to get a background check on the people entering our country.")
DFA 'strongly objects'
The DFA pushed back against Remulla's remarks, saying they undermined the agency's integrity and unfairly tarnished the reputation of the Philippine Foreign Service and its personnel.
The department said its authority to issue visas is grounded in both domestic and international law.
It cited Executive Order No. 292, or the Administrative Code of 1987, which recognizes visa issuance as a consular function, as well as the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations.
The DFA also explained that third-party providers such as VFS may perform administrative functions, including receiving visa applications, but do not have the authority to approve or deny them.
That authority remains with Philippine diplomatic missions, the department said.

"The visa fees collected are pursuant to applicable laws and regulations, including the prescribed Schedule of Fees. The DFA does not tolerate corruption and remains committed to accountability, transparency, and utmost professionalism in the delivery of public service," the DFA said. — with reports from Alyana Uy

articles.title: DFA rejects Ombudsman Remulla's call to outsource visa processing
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Monday pushed back against Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla"s call to strip the agency of its visa-issuance functions, rejecting his allegation that it had…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 10:35am

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Monday pushed back against Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla’s call to strip the agency of its visa-issuance functions, rejecting his allegation that it had turned the process into a business.
In a statement, the DFA said Remulla’s remarks “undermine the institutional integrity of the Department and unfairly malign the reputation of the Philippine Foreign Service and its personnel.”

“The visa fees collected are pursuant to applicable laws and regulations, including the prescribed Schedule of Fees. The DFA does not tolerate corruption and remains committed to accountability, transparency, and utmost professionalism in the delivery of public service,” the agency said.
The DFA also maintained that visa issuance involves substantive assessments of applications and verification of documents.

“These responsibilities require the exercise of official judgment pursuant to the applicable Philippine laws, rules and regulations, and cannot be reduced to just the administrative receipt and processing of documents,” it said.

Remulla earlier called for the government to outsource visa processing to a third-party service provider, arguing that visa issuance was an immigration concern that fell under the Department of Justice (DOJ).
He described visa processing as a clerical task and said the Philippines lacked the capacity to handle it effectively in other countries, making a third-party provider such as VFS a better option.

“The DFA’s problem is that it seems to have forgotten that its primary job is to be diplomats. In this case, they want something else to happen—they want to do business. They used to turn visa issuance in China into a business,” Remulla said on his program on DZRH.

Remulla was reacting to reports that the DFA was reviewing its policy on visa-free entry for Chinese tourists amid concerns that it may have contributed to the expansion of Philippine offshore gaming operator (POGO) activities.
In response, the DFA said its authority to issue visas is grounded in domestic law and international conventions.

While acknowledging that third-party providers such as VFS may offer administrative support services, the agency stressed that outsourcing these functions would not mean transferring the sovereign authority to approve or deny visa applications.
“This authority remains a governmental responsibility, as exercised by the Philippine Embassies and Consulates,” the DFA said.

“The DFA will continue to faithfully discharge its statutory responsibilities and uphold the integrity of Philippine visa issuance in the best interest of the country and the Filipino people,” it added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: UK police revisit 2019 claims on Thomas Markle amid Philippine probe
articles.summary: The Thomas Markle case has taken a new turn in London as a separate forensic examination is conducted in the Philippines.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 10:14am
In this screenshot, Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Duchess of Sussex Meghan, speaks in an interview with Australian morning show Sunrise in September 2021.
Sunrise on YouTube; Philstar.com screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — London's Metropolitan Police is reviewing how it handled allegations involving Thomas Markle in 2019, as Philippine investigators continue examining evidence recovered from his former home in Cebu.
The Met said it received a letter in January 2019 containing "a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom."
The force reviewed the letter and passed it to the office of Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, for their awareness, but did not share the allegations with other law enforcement agencies.
It is now reviewing how the matter was handled, including whether Britain's police watchdog should be called in.
Meghan said Friday, October 23, that she had been shown a letter containing "troubling and disturbing allegations" against her father and had been assured they were being investigated.
She initially said this occurred in 2018, but sources later clarified that she had misremembered the year and that the Met contacted her in 2019.
Laptop under examination
In the Philippines, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said police inspected Thomas Markle's former Cebu home after receiving a report from his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
"Found were a trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop," Remulla told Agence France Presse.
The laptop is undergoing forensic examination, with results expected within a week.
Remulla separately told The Guardian that investigators were considering all angles because of the family dispute surrounding the allegations.
"Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings," Remulla said.
He stressed that forensic analysis was still needed to provide a "definitive picture."
The interior secretary earlier told Agence France Presse that Philippine authorities would pursue "appropriate legal actions" if investigators find sufficient evidence.
Thomas Markle had been living in Cebu before reportedly returning to the United States for medical treatment earlier this year.
British reports said Thomas Markle Jr. discovered alleged child sexual abuse images among belongings at his father's former residence and reported them to Philippine authorities.
Admission on paid sex
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation said it was aware of the allegations and would "provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities."
The FBI also said it would investigate any related allegations of violations of US federal law.
Thomas Markle has denied possessing child sexual abuse material, calling the accusations "sick lies."
He also told the Daily Mail that computers cited in the allegations had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025.
Meghan said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations and hoped "justice will be fully served" while prioritizing the safety of children.
In a separate newspaper interview, Thomas Markle acknowledged that he had paid for sex while continuing to deny the child abuse allegations.
He told the Mail on Sunday, October 25 that he had "never had sex with anyone under the age of 18" and said that when he was single, he traveled to the Philippines at least twice and paid for sex.
UK-based Sky News, meanwhile, located Markle's former home in Cebu City describing it as a "fancy building."
"You've got marble floors, chandelier, it's not too far away from the sea front," Sky News reported. — with a report from Ian Laqui

articles.title: Philippines denies undersea cable arrangement with Taiwan
articles.summary: DFA says no cooperation arrangement exists after Beijing objected to the Washington discussion.

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 9:50am

Filipino soldiers walk along a beach in Calayan Island on June 30, 2023. Amid increasing geopolitical tension between the US, China, and Taiwan, the Philippines is grappling with the potential fallout. Batanes, a group of idyllic islands at the country’s northernmost tip, lies just 140 kilometers from Taiwan, and its proximity could thrust it into the spotlight in case of conflict.
Ezra Acayan / Pool / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has no arrangement with Taiwan to protect undersea cables, the Department of Foreign Affairs said on Monday, October 26, distancing the government from a Filipino diplomat’s remarks in Washington last week that Manila was exploring deeper cooperation with Taipei.

“There is no cooperative arrangement with Taiwan on subsea cables or other critical undersea infrastructure,” the department said in a short statement sent to reporters who had asked about the remarks.
The department affirmed that the country continues to adhere to its “longstanding and consistent One China Policy.”

Felipe Cariño III, deputy chief of mission at the Philippine Embassy in Washington, said during a seminar hosted by the Center for a New American Security that both countries were eyeing closer cooperation to jointly protect undersea cables, according to a Reuters report.

Cariño said the Philippines was taking a practical approach with Taiwan to protect shared interests in the Bashi Channel, the waterway between Batanes and southern Taiwan, and was doing so “notwithstanding our one China policy.”

The Filipino diplomat said the two sides were looking at knowledge-sharing and capacity-building, and that the cooperation could lead toward “addressing the gray-zone issues in our part of the world," according to the report.
When asked whether it could include joint patrols or holding vessels accountable for damaging cables, he said he did not have details.

The DFA however said the discussions during the forum centered on protecting critical undersea infrastructure through stronger public-private cooperation, mainly in repairing and recovering damaged facilities.
"It must be emphasized that the protection of [critical undersea infrastructure] requires concerted efforts by all parties that benefit from these essential networks," th department said.
"There was no mention of gray-zone activity cooperation with Taiwan," it added.

Beijing had been quick to react to the Filipino diplomat's remarks, with Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning saying a day after the forum that the Philippines should strictly adhere to the "one-China principle with real actions."
China views Taiwan as a breakaway province and has refused to rule out the use of force in bringing the self-ruled democracy under its control.

The Philippines shares the Luzon Strait with Taiwan, a waterway about 250 kilometres wide that links the Philippine Sea with the South China Sea. A total of 18 submarine cables pass through the strait, according to an analysis published this month by the Asia Pacific Network Information Centre.
The Batanes island chain spans most of the strait. Its northernmost island, Mavulis, lies about 140 kilometres from Taiwan’s southern tip.
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) in September accused Chinese research vessel Jia Hai Ke 7 of spoofing its location while holding position about 38 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat, Batanes.

It described its movements at the time as concerning, especially for "the security of the country's undersea communications infrastructure and the potential military use of the data collected," the PCG said.

image.caption: Lula has won Brazil’s presidential runoff against Bolsonaro, reversing his first-round defeat to the conservative candidateImage: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS

Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election

blocks.caption: Lula has won a fourth presidential term after a historic upset Image: Brian Snyder/REUTERS

blocks.text: Brazilian leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, electoral authorities said.

Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The campaign was marred by scandals and mudslinging. Sunday’s vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula’s claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.

Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.

In regards to foreign policy in his next term, Lula will have to manage relations with Washington while maintaining his anti-imperialist stance, as the Trump administration increasingly asserts its influence across the region. Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.

articles.title: India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted
articles.summary: Indian cartoonists say online restrictions are making satire harder, but they aren't giving up.

blocks.text: Image source, Satish Acharya
Satish Acharya is among Indian cartoonists whose work has been restricted by Meta recently
ByNikita Yadav
BBC News, Delhi
For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.
The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.

Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.

The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.
Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.
Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.
The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.
The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.
"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."

He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.
In a statement, Meta told the BBC that may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The message on Satish Acharya's profile when it was last blocked between 20-22 October

blocks.text: The message on Satish Acharya's profile when it was last blocked between 20-22 October
Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.

Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.

The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged ministers to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.
At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.

The Indian Express reported, external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.
The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.

Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.
The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.

Earlier this week, several media outlets reported, external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".
The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.

blocks.caption: Image caption, RK Laxman is among the most recognisable political cartoonists in India

blocks.text: Image source, India Today Group via Getty Images
RK Laxman is among the most recognisable political cartoonists in India
Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.
Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.

But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".
In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trivedi was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.

Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.
Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra, known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.
For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.
"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.
"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.
Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.
"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.
Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.

blocks.caption: Image caption, One of Manjul's cartoons which criticised the controversial voter roll revision that has resulted in the removal of 130 million names from the electoral rolls

blocks.text: Image source, Manjul
One of Manjul's cartoons which criticised the controversial voter roll revision that has resulted in the removal of 130 million names from the electoral rolls
Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.
"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.
But that freedom comes with a new vulnerability - dependence on platforms that can restrict their work or cut off access to their audiences.
No one knows this better than Rachita Taneja, the creator of the hugely popular Instagram comic Sanitary Panels.
"My career would not have existed without the internet," she told the BBC. Yet she describes social media as a double-edged sword.
"At the end of the day it's a for-profit endeavour that answers to advertisers," she says.
Taneja says that Meta's compliance with Indian government requests reflects the company's commercial priorities rather than concern for users' rights. Meta declined to comment.

Even cartoonists working in traditional newsrooms face pressure. Adhwaryu says artists may soften captions, avoid certain subjects or think twice before submitting a cartoon. Over time, he says, such self-censorship can become normalised, even without explicit instructions.
Still, cartoonists have found ways to support one another.

When Acharya's Instagram account was first restricted, Taneja drew a stick-figure cartoon in solidarity. "Seeing people on the front lines creating communities, protesting, running campaigns, tirelessly fighting for their own rights and the rights of others is what keeps me going," she says.
Adhwaryu believes satire will continue to adapt. He compares cartoons and humour to a "shape-shifting virus".
"It keeps mutating in response to its environment," he says. "It will find its way."

articles.title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
articles.summary:
The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty

When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he…

blocks.text: When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.

As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials prepare for an important meeting this week discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.

The “fifth plenum” starts on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.

As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.

Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.

Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.

Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.

blocks.caption: Xi Jinping at a gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing last week.  Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.

The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.

The upcoming meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.

Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.

In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.

In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.

Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.

Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.
