articles.title: Cabinet split emerges over controversial Rosebank oilfield decision
articles.summary:
Chancellor is in favour the North Sea project, but energy secretary has said she is leaning towards rejecting it

A cabinet split has emerged over whether to approve drilling at the Rosebank…

blocks.text: A cabinet split has emerged over whether to approve drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, with the chancellor, John Healey, in favour of the controversial North Sea project.

The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is ultimately in charge of the decision and the Guardian reported last week that she was leaning towards rejecting it after granting permission for the smaller Jackdaw gasfield.
It is understood, however, that Healey backs approving the licence, which is on hold over concerns about the project’s environmental impact.

The chancellor hinted at his support last week when he told ITV he expected oil and gas revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, suggesting he was anticipating income from Rosebank. The prime minister would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.
No 10 declined to comment on Sunday after the Mail on Sunday reported that both Andy Burnham and Healey had agreed to try to push the project through, saying it was a matter for the energy secretary.
Fahnbulleh is responsible, but the views of Burnham and Healey will hold weight in the choice over whether or not to go ahead.

She told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.

“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”
If the Rosebank field is rejected, it would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. A final decision is expected before the end of the year.

Labour MPs said on Wednesday that there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessary part of the transition to net zero.
MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved as a way of expressing dissent.

Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet made her decision. Rosebank would produce emissions about seven times greater than Jackdaw, and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given that most of the oil would be exported.
after newsletter promotion

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We do not comment on speculation. The North Sea remains a vital national asset, and oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come – alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.
“Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process.”

Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through an energy wealth fund. She said last week that the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.

“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.
She could not, however, say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

articles.title: Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola delays campaign stops after car crash
articles.summary: Peltola and her family sustained minor injuries after a driver struck the car transporting group to campaign stop

blocks.text: Mary Peltola, a Democrat who is running for Alaska’s lone US Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash while driving to a campaign stop on Saturday, her campaign said.

The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision.

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” Cheryl Bruce, Peltola’s campaign manager, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover.”

Bruce added: “Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families.”

Police responded to a “multi-vehicle collision” at about 6.55pm on Saturday, according to the Anchorage police department. Peltola’s family and the occupant of a second vehicle were taken to a local hospital “with non-life-threatening injuries”, according to the authorities, while the occupant of a third vehicle refused medical transport.

blocks.caption: Mary Peltola, center, celebrates with her family and supporters as ranked-choice tabulations were announced in November 2022 in Anchorage, Alaska. Photograph: Loren Holmes/AP

blocks.text: “The circumstances of the collision are under investigation,” reads a statement from the police department.

Peltola, an Alaska Native and former congresswoman, is challenging Republican incumbent senator Dan Sullivan, hoping to become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate. Both candidates have tried to rally support from Alaska Native voters, a key constituency in the high-stakes race that has become one of the most watched in the nation.

On Friday, Donald Trump ordered the justice department to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses. The lawsuit cites potential confusion with another Republican candidate who is listed on the ranked-choice ballot as Daniel J Sullivan Jr, who is a retired schoolteacher.
after newsletter promotion

Peltola’s incident delayed what her campaign announced as the “Alaska Always tour,” an eight-stop push through the last week before election day. Her campaign said she will resume events on Tuesday, with a stop in Homer, Alaska.

articles.title: Macron’s ‘vandals pay’ bill puts right to protest at risk
articles.summary:
Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents

Emmanuel…

blocks.text: Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves.

The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.

Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.

The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.

The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.

Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”.

The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.”
She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?”

Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.”

In an open letter to Le Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.”
At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.

At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage.

Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.”
He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.

Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.

articles.title: Brazil election 2026: Live second round results
articles.summary: After a shock defeat in the first round, the incumbent Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is seeking a new term in a runoff with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of his…

blocks.text: Polls close at 17.00 BRT, 20.00 GMT, with first results expected within the hour.
Live second round results

blocks.caption: LULA

blocks.text: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 0% Workers' party (PT) | 0 votes
Guardian graphic. Source: TSE
How the election works
Brazil’s president is elected purely by the popular vote. A winning candidate needs one more vote than 50% of votes cast; there is no role for the parliament and no electoral college.

Because no candidate achieved 50% in the first round on 4 October, the two leading candidates go into a runoff. One of them is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent leftwing president, commonly known as Lula. The other, and the leading candidate in the first round, is Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a failed coup attempt after he lost to Lula in the 2022 election, but has endorsed his son and hopes to be released if he wins. Bolsonaro junior is a lawyer and former senator from Rio.

In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the second round, with an electoral base concentrated in the north-east of the country, while Bolsonaro led in the south. But on that occasion Lula entered the second round as the leading candidate from the first round, and won the bellwether state of Minas Gerais, north of Rio de Janeiro. In the first round of the 2026 election, Bolsonaro beat Lula in Minas Gerais by 48.43% to 43.33%.

Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second vote. But Lula’s campaign has been buoyed by massive, student-led anti-Bolsonaro protests after the first round and hopes to stage a historic fightback on Sunday.
Lula is already the longest-serving president in Brazil’s modern history, serving two terms from 2003 to 2010, before returning to office in 2023. He will turn 81 on Tuesday. Bolsonaro is 45.

articles.title: North Vancouver graduates-to-be have a night to remember as party boat gets stuck in the mud
articles.summary: About 150 Sutherland Secondary School students who were celebrating their graduating year were stranded for hours on Friday night after their party boat ran aground in the Burrard Inlet.

image.caption: The Pride of Vancouver catamaran vessel ran aground in the Maplewood mudflats near the Ironworkers Memorial Bridge on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (Royal Canadian Marine Search and Rescue)

blocks.text: British Columbia
About 150 Sutherland Secondary School students who were celebrating their graduating year were stranded for hours on Friday night after their party boat ran aground in the Burrard Inlet.
Students say they felt scared, confused, but bonded because of it
About 150 North Vancouver students who were celebrating their graduating year were stranded for hours on Friday night after their party boat ran aground in the Burrard Inlet.
The Sutherland Secondary School students say they were only about two hours into a three-hour cruise when they got stuck.
Cady Nelson-Quine, student body president, says students weren’t completely evacuated until after midnight.
"People were super tired. They were using the tablecloth as blankets so they could fall asleep on seats," said Nelson-Quine.
The Pride of Vancouver catamaran vessel — operated by Spirit Cruises — was stuck in place near the Ironworkers Memorial Bridge, on the Maplewood mudflats, according to officials.
CBC News reached out to Spirit Cruises for comment but did not hear back by deadline.
Stuck in the mud

In a post to social media, the Royal Canadian Marine Search and Rescue said it was called in to help evacuate students and their chaperoning parents at 8:51 p.m., adding "the kids had a boat ride they likely won’t ever forget."
Nelson-Quine said a "loud gurgle" was heard over the loud music, coming from the bottom of the vessel when the boat stopped, which tilted on an angle when stuck.
There was some confusion and fear among passengers, added Nelson-Quine, until the Coast Guard arrived about an hour later.
The event was PAC-funded and organized by parents. (Submitted by Sally Cullen)
But as time went on, Nelson-Quine said the unique experience brought students together, even sparking new friendships, while some other students were comforted by their peers.
All passengers were safely transported to Vancouver’s Harbour Green Park, where they were met by their parents and guardians, according to search and rescue.
The Coast Guard said in an email no water entered the vessel after it ran aground. It deployed the Siyay hovercraft and safely evacuated all passengers.
The vessel’s crew remained on board, the agency said, until the vessel could be refloated with the rising tide early Saturday morning and then berthed in Coal Harbour.
Cut short

To reach the hovercraft, students and chaperones descended a ladder and walked roughly 20 metres across a fully exposed sandbar, Nelson-Quine said, which was difficult for some students wearing heeled shoes.
"They had to take them off and walk across all these barnacles and some of them were carried across the ground because of how sharp it was."
About 150 high school students and chaperoning parents were evacuated in two trips on a hovercraft. (Submitted by Cady Nelson-Quine)
But Catie Craven, graduating class president, said much of the cruise was spent eating, without a lot of time to dance and celebrate before it was cut short.
She said panic filled the room at first, and a lot of parents called the police after hearing the boat was tipped on an angle.
"It kind of just ruined the rest of the night for a lot of people," said Craven. "Some people are really annoyed about it, some people are upset."
Craven hopes another night of celebration will be arranged to make up for some lost time.
Organizers
Penny Gill, who attended the event as a parent chaperone, described the night as a "surreal experience."
"Did that really happen?" she said.
She said she got to see kids form new bonds and strengthen their relationships during a night "these kids will have forever."
Gill said she and another parent were among the last to be evacuated, and she didn't get home until 1 a.m.

In a statement, the North Vancouver School District said the event was not a school-sanctioned event, rather it was hosted by parent organizers and the school had no involvement in the planning of it.
The district said it is grateful for authorities who responded to the emergency and safely evacuated all passengers to shore.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.

articles.title: South Korean arrested for alleged ties to illegal gambling, says BI
articles.summary: A South Korean national was arrested by the Bureau of Immigration (BI) for his alleged involvement in illegal gambling activities linked to unauthorized online game servers operated in the country.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 3:08am
A South Korean national was arrested by the Bureau of Immigration (BI) for his alleged involvement in illegal gambling activities linked to unauthorized online game servers operated in the country.
BI Fugitive Search Unit (FSU) Chief Rendel Ryan Sy identified the fugitive as 41-year-old Lee Seunghyun, who was apprehended on October 13 in Barangay Western Bicutan, Taguig City.
Fugitive

In a statement, Sy said the arrest stemmed from a request from the South Korean government for Lee’s deportation to face charges in his home country. Lee is also reportedly the subject of an Interpol Red Notice.

"According to information provided by the South Korean Embassy, the Busan District Court issued an arrest warrant against Lee on January 15, 2026, after he was charged with violating South Korea’s Game Industry Promotion Act," the agency said.

"South Korean authorities allege that, beginning in January 2019, Lee and his accomplices manipulated an interface adapter to operate three unauthorized private online game servers in Angeles City, Philippines," it added.
Lee and his group collected cash payments from users in exchange for "Adena," the game's virtual currency through alleged unauthorized monetary transactions through the servers.
Overstaying

The records of the Bureau show that Lee arrived in the Philippines on July 26, 2018, and has remained in the country since then, making him an overstaying alien. He is also part of the Bureau’s blacklist since August 2019 as a fugitive from justice.
Lee is currently detained at the BI detention facility in Taguig City pending the finality of the deportation proceedings against him.

BI Commissioner Joel Anthony M. Viado said, “The Philippines will not be a safe haven for fugitives. Those wanted for criminal offenses abroad cannot use our country as a refuge from accountability. The BI will continue to track down foreign fugitives, enforce our immigration laws, and work with international partners to ensure that those sought by foreign authorities face the appropriate legal processes.” — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Emirati diplomat who helped deliver aid to Gaza enters UN secretary general race
articles.summary:
Lana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over the UAE’s human rights record and alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan

An Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN…

blocks.text: An Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN helped secure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza has entered the race as a late contender to succeed António Guterres as the world body’s secretary general.
Lana Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, is widely noted for her advocacy of the Palestinian cause and the two state solution and has won the endorsement of the state of Palestine.

She is however facing criticism over the UAE’s contested role in arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, a group that has been accused of genocide by two successive US administrations. Nusseibeh has been one of the leading UAE diplomats denying reports that the UAE supplied weapons to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo in defiance of a UN arms sales ban.

A grouping of Latin American and Caribbean states, CELAC, has also sent a letter of objection to the security council, claiming her late entry came just as a consensus was emerging behind their region holding the UN top job.

Nusseibeh, who was educated at Cambridge University, was born in 1978 in Abu Dhabi, where her father, Zaki, had emigrated after the Arab-Israeli 1967 war made it difficult for him to return to his birthplace, Jerusalem. She is the niece of Sari Nusseibeh, a distinguished Palestinian intellectual and author of a widely admired book on Palestine, Once Upon a Country.

She has justified her late – but widely predicted – entry into the race on the grounds that the UN security council appears to be close to deadlock on the six remaining candidates in the race, with no one as yet able to establish a clear lead after six rounds of voting, the latest on 16 October.

The latest straw poll – the first in which it was revealed whether any of the five permanent members of the 15-strong UN security council objected to a candidate – ended with Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica holding the lead spot.

But Gryspan faced objections from two unidentified permanent security council members, making it harder for her to claim she is a breakaway consensus candidate. She has support from nine security council members and objections from five. Guterres is due to stand down at the end of the year

Other candidates include the Argentine diplomat Rafael Grossi; the UN envoy from Guyana, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Olara Otunnu, a distinguished veteran Ugandan diplomat; and Ecuador’s former foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa. Two previously declared candidates have pulled out.
In her vision statement, Nusseibeh said: “At the heart of the UN sits a wager: that states will give up a little today to gain a great deal together over time.

“States have not stopped needing to partner with one another, but they no longer trust that cooperation will yield sufficient returns. Rebuilding that trust, with faster, more certain, and more realistic results, is the work of the UN.”

Brett McGurk, who served in the Biden administration as a top national security adviser, backed Nusseibeh for her work on Gaza. “How did UAE become the largest global provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to UN data? Because of Lana Nussaibeh – a diplomat who knows everyone and works with them … She would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat who heads Donald Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace, said Nusseibeh “has always understood that the UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build.”

He added: “In the Security Council [as UAE representative] she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism. She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN secretariat.”

But there is a fierce backlash from human rights activists who point to the UAE’s domestic human rights record and its alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan, the group responsible for killing thousands, including in the capture of El Fasher in October last year.
A January 2024 report by the UN panel of experts described allegations from sources in Chad and Darfur – including those of arms being smuggled into the RSF from the UAE – as credible.

One of the strongest attacks on Nusseibeh’s candidacy has been mounted by Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, over her denials of UAE provision of any “military, logistical, financial or political support to any faction in Sudan”. The UAE says it supports the formation of a civilian-led government in Sudan.

articles.title: Fisherfolk livelihood tied to West Philippine Sea amid disputes, says Archbishop Villegas
articles.summary: Beyond legal principles and politics, the dispute of the West Philippine Sea is affecting the livelihood and sustenance of fisherfolk who ride the waves on flimsy bancas and are up against the…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 2:49am

Beyond legal principles and politics, the dispute of the West Philippine Sea is affecting the livelihood and sustenance of fisherfolk who ride the waves on flimsy bancas and are up against the Chinese armed vessels and powerful ships, said Lingayen Dagupan Archbishop Socrates Villegas.

"Our people in Pangasinan are crying for help. I am their pastor. I am lending my voice to their groaning. Many of the people to whom my priests and I minister are fisherfolk for whom the West Philippine Sea means livelihood and sustenance for themselves and for the members of their families," said Villegas in a statement entitled "Setting our Feet on the Path of Peace: A Pastoral Moral Guidance for the Archdiocese of Lingayen Dagupan on the Issue of the West Philippine Sea."

"So it has been for decades past. The sea was what supported the humble fisherfolk of the Archdiocese of Lingayen Dagupan and the Dioceses of Iba and Alaminos. Its resources and wealth gave them and their families security. But they have never been greedy, never rapacious. They have taken from the sea only what they need!" he added.
Government leaders

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
However, China has refused to recognize the decision.
Recently, there has been a heated word exchange between Philippine and Chinese officials with some legislators urging that Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines be declared persona non grata.
On Friday, Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro said that if China forcefully towed away the sunken warship BRP Sierra Madre, it would be an act of war against the Philippines.

A report from a Chinese news outlet claimed that Beijing was mulling sanctions against Manila, including the towing of the BRP Sierra Madre—a World War II-era warship that was deliberately run aground in 1999 in Ayungin Shoal in the West Philippine Sea and continues to serve as an outpost for the country.

"'Yung Sierra Madre BRP, barko ng Republika ng Pilipinas ano at kung iyan ay tinangka, or, may mangyari diyan at sa kadahilanan ng ginamitan ng puwersa, eh, iyan ay act of war against the Republic of the Philippines," Teodoro said.

(The Sierra Madre BRP, it is a ship of the Republic of the Philippines, and if there is an attempt, or if something happened to it by force, that is an act of war against the Republic of the Philippines.)
Bancas against armed ships
Bishop Villegas, in his statement, expressed his support for Filipino leaders defending the country's territory.

"I stand firmly with those who assert Philippine sovereignty and insist on our sovereign rights over the maritime zones that prevailing law declares in our favor," said Villegas, adding that the issue is beyond legal principles and politics.
"It has to do with the livelihood of the fisherfolk in Pangasinan and Zambales, and the security of their future and that of their children. Do not forget the poor," he said.
Villegas said the flimsy bancas of fisherfolk are up against armed vessels and powerful ships.

"THIS IS A MORAL ISSUE. It has to do with justice as well as stewardship of creation, and IN THE NAME OF GOD, I ask the government to be firm and unyielding about what is lawfully ours and rightfully our people’s without provoking hostilities, but without cowering, however, in the face of the threat," the prelate said.

"The West Philippine Sea is God’s gift to His people. Its resources come from the Creator’s munificence and generosity. Defending it is taking the side of the people whom God has favored by the gift of the sea," he added. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine says its military did not violate Starlink terms, disputing Elon Musk claim
articles.summary: Ukrainian officials have disputed claims by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that the country's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite internet network for offensive drone…

image.caption: A firefighter tries to put out a fire at a shopping centre on Sunday following Russia's air attack in Kharkiv, Ukraine. Earlier this month, Ukrainian drones connected to Starshield lost connectivity at high speeds, disrupting air defences during daily Russian air attacks. (Andrii Marienko/The Associ

blocks.text: World·New

Ukrainian officials have disputed claims by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that the country's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite internet network for offensive drone strikes. Serhii Beskrestnov, a defence technology adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said long-standing restrictions on the civilian system in Ukraine made such offensive use impossible.
Ukrainian drones connected to Starshield lost connectivity earlier this month

Ukrainian officials have disputed claims by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that the country's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite internet network for offensive drone strikes.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a defence technology adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said long-standing restrictions on the civilian system in Ukraine made such offensive use impossible.
"It's very strange that Elon Musk doesn't know about the restrictions on Starlink's operation in Ukraine," he wrote in an online post.

SpaceX's Starlink and its military-focused Starshield service are critical to Ukraine's wartime connectivity. Earlier this month, Ukrainian drones connected to Starshield lost connectivity at high speeds, disrupting air defences during daily Russian air attacks. Officials said the so-called speed caps were lifted on Saturday, and the service was restored.
Still, questions have persisted about who ordered the interruptions to satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks .
Writing on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that drones operated via the civilian Starlink system had a speed restriction of 70 to 90 km/h within Ukraine and did not work in Russia.

Serhii Beskrestnov, also known as Flash, an adviser to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says it would not be possible for Ukraine's military to use Starlink for offensive drone strikes. (Efrem Lukatsky/The Associated Press)
"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes," he said.
Musk acknowledged on Saturday that SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication.
U.S. President Donald Trump has maintained that he didn't make that call, while Vice-President JD Vance has hinted at White House co-ordination with Musk.

items: Musk says he was behind Starlink speed restriction in Ukraine
Elon, Starlink and the betrayal of Ukraine

blocks.text: Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the Ukrainian military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
They also added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Trump's reported deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia that Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
New push to end the war
The restoration of Starlink service followed a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month.

On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by efforts from both first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on Western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors.
He said the attacks — many of them deadly — had affected nine regions of the country, damaging power plants, grain stores, civilian homes and commercial facilities.
Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine
More civilian deaths

Russia launched more than 20 attacks on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region overnight into Sunday, using drones and an aerial bomb, according to local authorities. Three people died at the scene and a fourth man later died in hospital, regional military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha reported, while over a dozen people were injured.

In Vinnytsia, a city in central Ukraine, at least six people were injured when a Russian drone struck a residential building, according to the state emergency service. The attack also damaged a nearby care home, with emergency crews evacuating 15 elderly residents, the service said.

Also according to the emergency service, consecutive Russian strikes on a shopping centre in Kharkiv injured four people late on Saturday, including three rescue workers. Ukraine has long accused Russia of so-called double-tap strikes, in which an initial attack is followed by another once rescuers arrive on the scene.
Firefighters work at the site of the shopping mall missile strike in Kharkiv on Saturday. (Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters)

Russia's Defence Ministry on Sunday claimed its forces targeted multiple sites in and around Kharkiv, including a shopping and logistics centre that it said had stored dual-use goods meant for the Ukrainian military.

In Russia, two people were killed and 13 others injured in Belgorod, a city 40 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, following "mass" nighttime drone strikes by Kyiv, regional Gov. Alexander Shuvayev reported on Sunday.

In the Russian city of Oryol, body of a fourth victim was pulled from the rubble the day after a Ukrainian strike on an industrial plant, local Gov. Andrey Klychkov reported. On Saturday, local authorities said three people had been killed in the attack.
Ukraine's general staff that day said its forces hit an electronics plant in Oryol that makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: Canada needs concrete results from EU summit this week, former envoy says
articles.summary: Ahead of this week's Canada-European Union summit, Prime Minister Mark Carney said both parties are hammering out a "new, ambitious alliance" after pledging deeper ties with Europe last month.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney participates in a news conference at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, in September. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
Ahead of this week's Canada-European Union summit, Prime Minister Mark Carney said both parties are hammering out a "new, ambitious alliance" after pledging deeper ties with Europe last month.
Stéphane Dion says Canada needs tangible results after hosting EU for 2-day summit in Montreal this week

Ahead of this week's Canada-European Union summit in Montreal, Prime Minister Mark Carney said both parties are hammering out a "new, ambitious alliance," after pledging deeper ties with Europe last month.

"An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens, and our citizens to do for themselves," Carney said in a written statement on Sunday. "An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices, and an alliance open enough that others can join.”
Former Liberal leader Stéphane Dion — who was special envoy to the EU from 2017 to 2025 — made clear that Canada needs to come out of this week's summit with nothing short of something tangible.

"What we need to see now is concrete results in all these files: trade, science, defence and security, artificial intelligence — concrete results of this partnership we have with the EU," Dion told CBC's David Common on Rosemary Barton Live Sunday morning.
"If it's, again, a kind of a communiqué at the end that would say 'we will continue to continue,' that would be very depressing."
Dion pointed to student and professional mobility between Canada and the EU as another area of improvement.
In his speech to the European Parliament last month, Carney showed clear interest in Erasmus+, a popular European exchange program that includes students and workers.
Stéphane Dion speaks to reporters at the Canadian Embassy in Paris on Feb. 10, 2025. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)
Dion also said he wants to see action to put Canada's existing free trade deal with the EU — the Canada-European Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) — into full effect.

CETA was signed in 2016 and most of the agreement, aside from its investment chapter, took effect provisionally in 2017. All member states need to approve CETA for it to take full effect and, as of now, nine EU member states have not ratified the treaty in their respective legislatures: Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy and Poland.

Ahead of the summit, Canada and the EU are working on a digital trade agreement to ease business transactions across borders by smoothing frictions around e-signatures and e-contracts, paperless trade, secure cross-border data flows, duties on electronic transmissions and e-commerce.

items: Carney wants Canada to join Europe's Erasmus+ program. What is it?
Carney says Europe, Canada aren't 'fair-weather allies' while rebuking Trump's tactics

blocks.text: A new kind of partnership
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the first "associate member" of the EU.
Carney welcomed the proposal's "ambition," but opted for the term "alliance of the future," when he spoke to the European Parliament a day later.
Canadian ambassador focused on 'results' after EU chief opens door to associate membership
"I'm not sure that this expression of an associate membership will fly," Dion said, noting that the term is up against resistance both in Canada and Europe.

"It sounds like if Canada was sending part of its sovereignty to Brussels, and there is no appetite for that in Canada," Dion continued. "In Europe, it's like if Canada would have the advantages of the union without the obligations that come with it regarding financing, regarding regulation alignment."

Dion instead suggested Canada could become an "official observer," offering reciprocity to the bloc while protecting Canadian interests. Observers have a limited membership where they can't vote or fill an elected position within the European Parliament's organization.
He also said an improvement to the Canada-EU partnership would be full membership in the European Political Community, a forum where European countries beyond the member states meet twice a year.

Dion said the European Political Community "would welcome Prime Minister Carney as the most European of non-European countries," and Canada could take part without commitments like financing or regulatory alignment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: US south-west braces for more flooding after stretch of heavy rain and storms
articles.summary:
More inclement weather forecast in rain-soaked Four Corners region after evacuations and rescues last week

A rain-soaked swath of the south-west US braced on Sunday for

blocks.text: A rain-soaked swath of the south-west US braced on Sunday for another round of potentially heavy showers and thunderstorms after days of rain forced evacuations and water rescues.

The National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of the Four Corners – the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah – even as local officials forecast further receding of swollen rivers that surged since rains picked up on Wednesday.

About 4ft (1 meter) of water flooded the home of Shane Ferrari, the sheriff of San Juan county, New Mexico. He said the area’s situation was stable on Sunday, but he and other residents were trying to clean up and deal with damage.
San Juan county spokesperson Devin Neeley said the county did not have official numbers on damage to homes or the number of people evacuated, but he was not aware of any loss of life.

blocks.caption: Flooding in the Gould Wash drainage watercourse in Hurricane, Utah, on Thursday. Photograph: Landon Christensen/AP

blocks.text: Neeley said the flood waters were receding but left mud and silt, much of which has been contaminated with sewage because of failures at waste plants. There were still power outages affecting multiple areas, and it would probably be a few days until residents got their power back on.
“It’s a pretty active disaster zone,” he said. “We’re not on the downswing by any means.”

The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and areas of New Mexico.

blocks.caption: Pickup trucks are submerged along Highway 160 in South Fork, Colorado, on Friday. Photograph: South Fork Fire Rescue/AP

articles.title: 'We have to fight back': Ombudsman urges public to speak up vs. gov't abuses
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla urged the public to openly communicate concerns about and abuses by the government.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 1:26am

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla urged the public to openly communicate concerns about and abuses by the government, affirming his office’s commitment to “stand alongside the Filipino people in fighting for their rights.”
In a press release issued Sunday, Remulla said that the fight against corruption and abuse of power requires a collective effort between the government and the public.

“We try to make accountability something felt by the people who matter, and the people who matter is the Filipino people. Tayong mga Pilipino, dapat kaya nating isaayos ang bayan natin at kaya nating lumaban para sa ating mga karapatan. We have to fight for our rights,” the Ombudsman said.

(We try to make accountability something felt by the people who matter, and the people who matter are the Filipino people. As Filipinos, we must be able to put our nation in order and fight for our rights. We have to fight for our rights.)
“... We have to fight back by being open or by openly communicating to us what is happening on the ground,” he added,
The Ombudsman said that it recognizes the importance of gathering information from citizens to identify and address abuses and weaknesses in government public services.

Remulla urged the public not to tolerate or accept public servants who abuse their position, adding that the Office of the Ombudsman serves as an avenue for citizens to demand accountability when officials misuse their authority.
“If we accede to the antics of many people in government who have a wrong idea of how to exercise power and responsibility, then things will never improve,” Remulla said.
Under the Constitution, the Office of the Ombudsman is mandated to act on complaints filed against public officials and employees, ensuring accountability in public office. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela
articles.summary:
Nobel peace prize winner’s return after almost a year in exile is unlikely to please interim president Delcy Rodríguez

The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has announced…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has announced she has returned to Venezuela almost a year after she left the country to receive the Nobel peace prize.
“I’m here. With you,” she wrote on X on Sunday lunchtime.

Her close ally Edmundo González, who is in exile, confirmed her arrival. “Venezuela! I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil,” he posted on social media.
“Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!” He added that he too would soon return.

It was not immediately clear how Machado, 59, had managed to return to Venezuela but footage on social media showed she was in Barquisimeto, the capital of Lara state, which is about 220 miles west of the capital, Caracas.
Images showed Machado surrounded by supporters holding mobile phones in a church called the Sanctuary of the Divine Shepherdess.

The Trump administration had reportedly opposed Machado’s return to Venezuela, believing her presence would complicate the cosy relationship it has struck up with the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, since abducting her former boss, the dictator Nicolás Maduro, in January.
Machado and Rodríguez are arch political rivals.

Machado slipped out of Venezuela last December – a few weeks before Maduro’s capture – and in recent months has reportedly made more than half a dozen failed attempts to return home, including after the devastating earthquake that hit the northern coast in June.

After Maduro was seized many had expected Trump to give Machado his blessing to take power. Her movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, although he refused to hand over power.
Instead Trump embraced Rodríguez, Maduro’s vice-president, who now governs a country widely seen as a US protectorate.

articles.title: Lacson, Gatchalian urge peaceful arrest of Bato
articles.summary: Senators are urging law enforcers to ensure a peaceful and bloodless arrest of fugitive Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, even as the chamber’s leadership rejected the idea of…

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 1:00am
Protesters stage a rally at the Senate on May 13 this year.

MANILA, Philippines — Senators are urging law enforcers to ensure a peaceful and bloodless arrest of fugitive Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, even as the chamber’s leadership rejected the idea of negotiating with the armed group reportedly protecting him.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian told dzBB yesterday that operations must prioritize the safety of both Dela Rosa and the arresting officers, especially amid warnings from the Department of the Interior and Local Government regarding potential violence and up to 10,000 possible casualties.
Sen. Panfilo Lacson echoed this sentiment, defending Dela Rosa’s right to due process as he faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC).
“I sincerely hope and pray that should his arrest take place sooner or later, it will be carried out peacefully, without violence or tragedy,” Lacson said.
While stressing he is not fully aware of the details surrounding the armed group protecting Dela Rosa, Gatchalian opposed any move to broker deals with the senator’s armed protectors.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla earlier said the government was initiating conversations with Dela Rosa’s “powerful” protectors for his turnover to authorities.
“That is not right because the government should not negotiate with an armed group,” Gatchalian argued.

“Because if you are armed and you are not authorized to bear arms, for me you are like a terrorist and a criminal group. So, the government should not negotiate with terrorists and criminal groups... it seems like the government is weak (if it does that),” he added.
The government recently placed a P50-million bounty on Dela Rosa and issued a one-week surrender ultimatum.
However, Lacson questioned the logic behind the multimillion-peso reward if authorities truly have solid intelligence on the senator’s whereabouts.
“If they really know where he is, why is there a need to post a P50-million bounty?” he asked.
He also dismissed speculations that the manhunt is a politically timed maneuver to prevent Dela Rosa from voting in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Lacson noted that the Senate already formally ruled to exclude fugitive senators beyond its coercive power from the voting denominator.
Government using Bato issue

Meanwhile, Tindig Pilipinas co-convenor Kiko Aquino Dee questioned Remulla’s handling of the arrest warrant against Dela Rosa, accusing the Marcos administration of using the case to distract the public from other issues.
Speaking at a rally in Makati, Dee said the government had issued strong warnings against Dela Rosa despite the pending ICC arrest warrant.

“Dela Rosa was supposed to be arrested in May. Now, suddenly, there is this new ploy. Jonvic Remulla is making alarming statements about Bato. This is a signature move of the Marcos administration: they create a diversion on one side while robbing us on the other,” Dee said.

Dela Rosa, a former Philippine National Police chief, has been named a co-conspirator of former president Rodrigo Duterte in the ICC’s crimes against humanity case related to the war on drugs. — Mark Ernest Villeza

articles.summary: Opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado reappeared in Venezuela Sunday for the first time since December, about a month before the U.S. military deposed the country's then-President…

image.caption: Supporters of Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado gather to demand that a date be set for presidential elections, in Caracas on Thursday. (Ariana Cubillos/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado reappeared in Venezuela Sunday for the first time since December, about a month before the U.S. military deposed the country's then-President Nicolás Maduro.
Machado went into hiding in Venezuela for 11 months after being briefly detained following protest

Opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado reappeared in Venezuela on Sunday for the first time since December, about a month before the U.S. military deposed the country's then-president Nicolás Maduro.
Machado announced her arrival on social media, writing: "I am here. With you."
Meanwhile, Venezuela's opposition leader Edmundo Gonzalez wrote on X confirming that Machado had arrived and that he would be next to her "very soon."
"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" he wrote. "You know it, this is until the end."
Machado's homecoming after more than 10 months in exile took place as doubts over Venezuela's democratic future — and the U.S.'s role in it — deepen.
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader
Since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela has been run by interim President Delcy Rodríguez, a longtime Maduro ally who received the Trump administration's blessing to succeed him.
Rodríguez has exceeded the time she was authorized to serve as acting president following Maduro's capture, and no election is scheduled.

items: Venezuelans of all stripes are denouncing Trump's 'biggest oil deal ever'

blocks.text: Machado went into hiding in Venezuela for 11 months after being briefly detained following a protest in January 2025.
After leaving the country in a clandestine escape, she reappeared that December in Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her peaceful challenge to Maduro's authoritarian government.
Machado and her allies have been demanding a date for a presidential election in Venezuela, but U.S. officials have emphasized economic stabilization first.

articles.title: Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
articles.summary: Machado had left the country just a month before the US government seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

blocks.text: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after over 10 months in exile.
"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday.

Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González Urrutia, confirmed the news minutes later, writing: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil."
In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro.
The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader, and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal with the US.

articles.title: Serbia votes as strongman Vučić faces grassroots challenge to 12-year rule – Europe live
articles.summary: The Student List movement is taking on authoritarian leader following nearly two years of protests against government and institutional corruption

blocks.text: Key events

items: 15m agoWho is Aleksandar Vučić?
28m agoBlog opening: Serbia's strongman Vučić faces sternest test of his 12-year rule

blocks.text: Who is Aleksandar Vučić?

Serbia’s former president and now prime ministerial candidate (again) Aleksandar Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo.

blocks.caption: Serbia's former president and the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vučić speaks to the media during the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters

blocks.text: He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. His Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, has been in government since 2012.

He first spent three years as the prime minister from 2014, before switching to the role of the president in 2017. Unable to run for the third term, he resigned from the post in September, and now wants to lead the government again.

As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.
He maintains close ties with Putin’s Russia and Xi’s China, which regularly gets him criticism from the EU and complicates Serbia’s path to the bloc.

blocks.caption: Russian president Vladimir Putin meets with his Serbian counterpart Aleksandar Vučić in Sochi in November 2021. Photograph: Mikhail Klimentyev/SPUTNIK/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Serbia has regressed in international rankings for press freedom and corruption in recent years, and its process of joining the EU is effectively stalled. More on that shortly.

Vučić is also fairly close with Donald Trump and his associates. He hosted Donald Trump Jr and Jared Kushner in Belgrade, and, as we revealed, personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal – and definitely very controversial – scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower.
Blog opening: Serbia's strongman Vučić faces sternest test of his 12-year rule

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Dobro veče, or good evening, and welcome to our live coverage of Serbian election night.

blocks.caption: People vote as Serbia holds parliamentary elections in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/Getty Images

blocks.text: The grassroots protest movement, the Student List, is taking on the country’s increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić, in what is shaping up to be the sternest test of his 12-year grip on power.

The vote is a culmination of two years of student-led protests triggered by the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy in November 2024, which killed 16 people and uncovered massive government and institutional corruption.

The bottom-up leaderless movement, with 250 candidates democratically elected from people with limited political experience but distinguished professional careers, seeks to end Vučić’s rule and rewire the state, with focus on fighting alleged corruption, clientelism and power abuses of the past.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Serbia’s student-led movement attend the final campaign rally in central Belgrade on Thursday. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Polls opened at 7am (6am UK time) and close at 8pm (7pm UK time). Until then, we’ll bring you all the key background, explain why it matters for Europe, Ukraine, and you, and give you a flavour of the chatter in the queues outside polling stations from Belgrade to London.
I will also keep one eye on the first round of the presidential election in Bulgaria, so expect an odd update on this or two on this.
Ready? Let’s go. Ajde.
It’s Sunday, 25 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good evening.

articles.title: Ali G: Who Iz I? stooge says he was in on joke but didn’t tell Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘He’s not going to punk me. I’ll trick him’
articles.summary: Exclusive: Joshua Loudermilk says suspicions first raised during filming by gun shaped like wearable plastic bottom: ‘You’re gonna put a butt on top of a butt? You can’t run in…

blocks.text: Joshua Loudermilk, one of two men apparently discredited by the new Ali G movie Ali G: Who Iz I?, has said that he was in on the joke, but that the film-makers didn’t realise this.

Loudermilk, a 54-year-old aspiring actor from North Carolina, has told the Guardian he recognised star Sacha Baron Cohen early in the shoot but continued pretending to be a hard-right Maga sympathiser prepared to defend the US border at all costs.

The movie involves Loudermilk being recruited by another Cohen character, the ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, to help form a citizens’ warrior force to protect US borders, making use of his top-secret new weapon: a gun disguised as buttocks.

Along with fellow recruit Michael Aboud, the chair of the El Paso county Republican party, Loudermilk joins Morad on a mission to stop the birth on US soil of the baby of a fictional South American drugs kinpin. This involves abducting a woman apparently in labour, abandoning her in a deserted medical facility, kidnapping her newborn child (a lifelike prosthetic) and driving it in a zipped bag to the border in order to deliver it by drone to Mexico.

Aboud is shown taking the decision to drop the child from a great height into Mexico rather than have it touch US soil. He has since called Cohen a “liar” and a “pervert” and expressed his intention to sue. The film repeatedly stresses that both men were “not in on it”.

Loudermilk has told the Guardian he was surprised the production company did not notice social media updates he posted shortly after the shoot in which he named Cohen and expressed his excitement about the project.

But rather than being upset about his involvement, Loudermilk – who recently appeared as Squire Dap in the North Carolina Town of Hudson Fall Dinner Theatre’s production of Camelot – says he welcomes the publicity boost.

“I want to use this to my benefit,” he says. “I would hope Sacha would read this and laugh, like: ‘Hey, you got me!’ I had so much fun creating that character. I was trying to see if I was any good at acting in comedy. And I realised: ‘Oh, I think I’m good at this.’ And that’s what I wanna do for the rest of my life.”

blocks.caption: Joshua Loudermilk. Photograph: Joshua Loudermilk

blocks.text: His experience began in September 2025 when Loudermilk spotted a post on Craigslist by a body called the American Citizen Initiative (whose website is no longer active) recruiting “patriotic legal Americans” “concerned about the border crisis” who “believe that illegal immigration is out of control”.

The ad, one of dozens posted across US states simultaneously, invited “real American citizens” to “attend an exclusive, hands-on event experience where you’ll learn the truth about what’s happening on the border and how you can make a difference”. Attendees were promised $300 as well as travel expenses.
“I was like: this seems kind of weird,” says Loudermilk, who describes himself as broadly apolitical. “I don’t really care much about our borders. My mom’s from Ireland.”

Recently made redundant, his motivation for responding was primarily financial. “I know rightwing and leftwing organisations have money and will pay people to just hold a sign up. I remember thinking: I wanna get on that gravy train. I want some George Soros money. I’ll pretend to be whatever. Just let me feed my family. It could have been save the whales and I would have done it.”

In his application, Loudermilk fabricated hard-right views, mentioned that he had been a preacher and neglected to declare his ambitions to become a comedy actor – in part, he says, out of embarrassment. He then filled in a “silly questionnaire – very obvious, very slanted to the right”.

Loudermilk was then called for a video interview, which involved the identification of left-leaning celebrities, as well as figures including Borat, Cohen’s bumbling Kazakh reporter, who Loudermilk duly named.

He was also asked if he was a Trump supporter. “The funny thing is: not really. He’s just a leader. But I was like: I’m going to be an improv actor so I said: ‘Yeah, I support Trump!’ Next thing I know they’re like, ‘We want you to come out to be a part of this.’

The company flew him to Ontario, California, with an initial offer of $1,000, plus food and expenses, on top of which Loudermilk received a further $700. “It was all real secretive. They frisked me down and I got in a truck to go to a karate studio.”

Once he arrived, Loudermilk was greeted by security and informed an Israeli commander wanted to meet him. “That was a red flag. Why would Israeli commander be in America? I go in there and immediately I see this really tall guy with this horrible plastic surgery. My first thought was: that looks like Sacha Cohen. But I was like: nah, that can’t be him.”

blocks.caption: Sacha Baron Cohen as ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad in the 2018 show Who is America? Photograph: Showtime

blocks.text: Loudermilk’s suspicions were further raised, he says, when he met his fellow recruits. “They were old, old, old white guys who were really out of shape. Everyone’s wearing these Trump shirts. They didn’t seem like warriors. I thought: they could probably get better people for this.”

Morad then produced the top-secret new gun in the shape of large, strap-on bottom, out of which bullets are fired from the anus. Initially, Loudermilk was baffled by its logistics. “I kept thinking: no-one’s gonna wear that thing because your butt’s gonna be abnormally large. No one has a butt like that. Are you gonna put a butt on top of a butt? You can’t run in that. And you’d have to wear some really big khaki pants.”

He volunteered to be first to try the weapon out, whereupon Morad demonstrated the trigger system, which involves the pumping of an attached rubber penis. “And he kept calling it ‘shmeckel’. I’m like: that’s Sacha Cohen. At that moment I knew it.

“And I was like: oh no, I can’t break character. I’ve got to go along with it. So what I decided [was] that whatever he did, I was going to take it another step further. He’s not going to punk me; I’m going to trick him. So I decided to get into character and just have a good time because they’re paying me.”

As the plot became more “ridiculous”, says Loudermilk, so his enjoyment increased. During a scene in which he, Morad and Aboud help deliver the (prosthetic) baby, the three men become covered with fake excrement. “This big blast of pooping pap,” recalls Loudermilk – but he was reassured after inadvertently sampling some of the fluids. “I thought: ‘This doesn’t taste bad.’ So I just kind of hung in there. It was disgusting, but I was having fun.”

blocks.caption: Loudermilk and Aboud in Ali G: Who Iz I? Photograph: Ali G: Who Iz I?

blocks.text: At the climax at the Mexican border, says Loudermilk, he handed the remote control to the drone to Aboud, “because that was boring. It was ridiculous – they’re not flying a real baby”. Instead, he “wanted to have fun with Sacha,” so he grabbed the “butt-gun”, yelling about the need to defend themselves, and eventually discharged fire, aided by Morad, who helps pump the penis trigger.
Loudermilk declines to defend Aboud’s decision to then endanger the life of the baby by dropping it from the drone, but expresses some sympathy for his unwitting co-star.

“I felt sorry for the poor fella. Because I’m all-in and he’s just kind of following me around like in a daze, like: what’s happening? He was scared to death, and obviously very uncomfortable, bless his heart.

“I’d never met the guy before, but [at times] it felt he was totally freaking out on me. So I had to make him believe that I believed all this. So I would tell him, ‘You’re being a wimp, man. Our freedom is on the line.’ I kept trying to keep him from quitting.
“But I’m surprised he didn’t figure it out. Like, come on, Michael – why would they recruit you to defend our border? Think about it.”

Loudermilk concedes his decision to maintain the pretence of being far-right once he had worked out the true nature of the project was in part because he “was a little offended. Like: really? You’re picking on these Americans that aren’t the brightest. You’re gonna make fun of them and they’re not gonna know any better. So I decided I needed to be their ally, even though I’m not that way.”

blocks.caption: Baron Cohen at the film’s Los Angeles premiere.  Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/Reuters

blocks.text: At the end of filming, Loudermilk signed a non-disclosure agreement at the request of the production company, which he says he was not given a copy of, and which mostly related to the top-secret weapons. “They came up to me after I was done and said, ‘Oh, you did so well!’ I said, ‘You get what you need? Can I talk about it?’ They said, ‘Oh no, not yet. Especially the butt-gun.’”

Loudermilk considers any such terms breached now the film is out and mentions him by name: “It’s fair game.” He adds that, after shooting, he had some qualms about not coming clean to them that he had twigged. “I felt a little bad. And that’s why I thought: I should make a little post.”

In December last year, Loudermilk posted three times on his public Facebook page about “eight hours of intense filming one on one with Sasha [sic] Cohen”, as well as twice on his Instagram, which is also public.
“But they never saw it. And the fact they missed that makes it even better to me. So I guess it’s on them.”
Last week, representatives for the film confirmed again to the Guardian that Loudermilk was not in on the joke. They have not yet responded to a further followup question on this.

The film was released nationwide in the UK on Friday, as well as in a limited run in the US. Loudermilk, who has not yet watched it, says he is unconcerned about the prospect of recriminations from anyone upset by his apparent actions.
“That people would be disgusted is a compliment. Oh, I really did a good job, huh! I pulled it off and I was so proud of myself.”

articles.title: Protein shakes for teenagers: Good or bad idea?
articles.summary: Protein products are marketed as a way of building muscle and losing weight — and they're very popular with young people. They also claim to promote healthy growth in children. Is this true? How much…

image.caption: Do we need protein shakes if we do a lot of sport?Image: Monkey Business 2/Shotshop/picture alliance

blocks.text: You can take it as a powdered drink, or in a snack bar. Puddings and certain breads are also promoted as "sources of protein," and protein-enriched products like Kindershake and Teen Balance are specifically designed to appeal to a young people — and it appears to be working.

In a representative survey of almost 1,000 parents by the University of Michigan in 2024, just under half said their children, who were aged 13 to 17, had consumed protein products over the previous year. The survey found that boys were more likely to do so than girls, especially in connection with sport, or to build muscle. Girls took them to balance their diet, and to lose weight.
According to the statistics portal Statista, between March 2024 and March 2025 the fitness protein product market in Germany recorded a huge jump of around 25% in retail revenue.
How much protein do we actually need?

Proteins are key building blocks for our metabolism. They play an important role in building up and repairing tissue in our muscles, skin and organs. Proteins are the basis for the formation of enzymes that regulate chemical reactions in the body, and of antibodies that are vital for our immune system.

According to the German Nutrition Society (DGE), healthy adults should consume 0.8 grams of protein daily per kilogram of body weight. A woman weighing 65 kilos should eat 52 grams of protein per day, for example.

But they can do this without special protein products. A portion of oat flakes with an almond drink for breakfast, a baked potato with curd cheese for lunch, and two slices of wholemeal bread with peanut butter in the evening — objective achieved.

Young people should consume a little more, as they are still growing. For them, the formula is 0.9 grams of protein per kilo of body weight. A teenager weighing 45 kilos should therefore eat 40.5 grams of protein per day. People over 65 and children aged one to four should have a little more: one gram of protein per kilo of body weight.

Older people tend to eat too little protein, often because their appetite decreases. But a study done in Germany between 2015 and 2017 showed that children and young people there often consume too much. Around half of six- to 17-year-olds ate more than double the recommended daily amount of protein.
Can too much protein be dangerous?

Too much protein can be harmful in the long term, according to the DGE. Various studies show that children who eat too much protein, particularly animal protein, often become overweight. Some enter puberty early.

blocks.caption: Eating too much protein can cause people to become overweight and lead to health problemsImage: yurakrasil - stock.adobe.com

blocks.text: Above all, too much protein can put excessive strain on the kidneys, causing damage. The kidneys have to convert the amino acids that constitute the building blocks of proteins into urea before they are excreted in urine. Damage is particularly likely if a person doesn't drink enough fluids, or has pre-existing kidney damage — but adolescents are also at greater risk.
Protein helps build muscle and shed weight

A person's protein requirement is greater if they are very physically active. Among other things, according to a DGE position paper, proteins can help maintain or build up muscular mass and strength, and support recovery after strain.

The paper states that, depending on physical condition and what they are training for, sportspeople should consume between 1.2 and 2 grams of protein per kilo of body weight, divided into several portions throughout the day. These recommendations only apply to people who train for more than five hours a day.

Proteins are of interest to people who want to lose weight because they are good at satisfying hunger. People usually lose more weight by following a protein-rich diet rather than another. Long-term, though, the most important thing to look at is: How many calories am I consuming, and how many am I burning?
Is animal protein better than plant protein?
Overall, plant proteins usually contain somewhat fewer essential amino acids than animal protein. "Essential" because the body cannot make them by itself – it has to take them in as food.
Vegetarian protein for muscle building

However, wholegrain products, pulses, or nuts are also higher in fiber, vitamins, and unsaturated fats – all of which are healthy. The DGE therefore advises that protein intake should be increased primarily with sources of plant protein.
What is the criticism leveled against protein products?

Protein powders and bars are often enriched not only with vitamins and minerals but also with unhelpful ingredients like sweeteners, sugar, additives and flavorings. The German Sport University in Cologne even found doping substances in protein products that were praised for building muscle.

Adolescents in particular might experience an unpleasant side-effect of consuming protein powders. These usually consist of milk proteins. There are various ways in which milk proteins can increase the skin's production of sebum, and this can trigger or exacerbate acne, although a direct link between milk protein products and acne has not been definitively proven.

blocks.caption: Protein powder made from whey: Around 200 liters of milk are needed for one kilogram of powderImage: Carballo/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Specialists are also skeptical about protein shakes, fearing that they could lead to young people eating fewer normal meals, and thus consuming less fiber, micronutrients, and healthy fats.
'High protein content' = higher price

Protein-enriched foods are usually expensive. In a 2022 study, consumer organizations also found that foods that are naturally high in protein, such as cheese, curds, or soya drinks, often cost more if the protein content has been highlighted by the manufacturer.

Not even sportspeople with a high protein requirement need to supplement their diet with special protein products. The DGE advises that they should aim to satisfy their requirements by optimizing their diet, and says there is no scientific evidence that our bodies require protein-enriched food supplements when put under strain.
However, the experts do say that it may make sense for people to use protein preparations if they have allergies, problems with digestion, chewing, or swallowing, or if their appetite is very low.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: UN flags military use of AI
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being given a growing number of responsibilities in military affairs, and the role of human judgment in military operations is shrinking rapidly, the head of the…

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Artificial intelligence (AI) is being given a growing number of responsibilities in military affairs, and the role of human judgment in military operations is shrinking rapidly, the head of the United Nations’ independent disarmament research institute warned.

United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR) Director Robin Geiss said on Tuesday that AI is being widely used on the battlefield and AI was increasingly “on track to crowding out human decision-making” in the sector.
“Crucially, this comes at the expense of human judgement, including in the nuclear domain,” Geiss said.
Many of these evolving AI systems are opaque, and the UNIDIR chief warned they are increasing the risk of error, miscalculation and therefore of unintended escalation.
